meta.title: Hyliion Holdings — Thomas Healy's KARNO Power Module through the Hypertruck pivot, Argonne National Lab linear-motor heritage, and the AI data center distributed-power thesis
meta.abstract: Hyliion Holdings Corp. (NYSE: HYLN) is a Cedar Park, Texas-headquartered distributed-power technology company that pivoted in 2023 from its founding hybrid/electrified Class 8 commercial truck powertrain thesis (Hypertruck ERX) to focus exclusively on the KARNO Power Module — a fuel-agnostic linear-motor electric generator originally developed at Argonne National Laboratory under DOE funding and acquired by Hyliion in 2022. The KARNO platform claims fuel flexibility (natural gas, hydrogen, ammonia, broader hydrocarbons), high electrical efficiency, low NOx emissions, and modular deployment scalability — positioning the technology for distributed power generation, AI data center backup/bridge power, microgrid integration, and broader stationary power applications. Strategic narrative through 2024-2026 centers on (a) post-Hypertruck strategic pivot execution, (b) KARNO product commercialization timeline, (c) AI data center distributed-power thesis activation and customer engagement, (d) capital structure adequacy through pre-revenue scaling, and (e) the founder-CEO Thomas Healy continuing leadership through the multi-year strategic transition.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## The Distributed-Power Thesis

The artificial-intelligence infrastructure boom of 2024 and 2025 produced an unexpected constituency for a small Cedar Park, Texas company that had spent its first eight years trying to electrify eighteen-wheelers. As hyperscalers raced to commission GPU clusters faster than regional transmission operators could build new interconnections, a gap opened for behind-the-meter distributed generation — reliable, permit-light, fuel-flexible power that could land on a data center campus ahead of the grid. Hyliion Holdings (NYSE: HYLN) had, by late 2023, bet its entire corporate identity on a technology that claimed to fill precisely that gap.

The company Thomas Healy founded in 2015, while finishing a graduate engineering programme at Carnegie Mellon University, was originally nothing of the sort. Hyliion's founding thesis was hybrid electrification of Class 8 commercial trucks — a bolt-on rear-axle motor system branded the Hypertruck ERX. The product attracted enough institutional attention to justify a de-SPAC merger with Tortoise Acquisition Corp, which closed in October 2020 and landed Hyliion on the New York Stock Exchange with a balance sheet flush from the SPAC trust. For two years the company pursued the commercial-trucking market, soliciting fleet orders and building manufacturing relationships.

## The KARNO Pivot

The thesis changed in October 2022 when Hyliion acquired a linear-motor generator technology from GE Additive. The underlying science had originated at Argonne National Laboratory under Department of Energy funding — a thermoacoustic generator in which a linear motor converts heat directly into electricity without rotating parts, crankshafts, or combustion chambers in the conventional sense. GE Additive had held the intellectual property but not commercialised it. Healy saw a platform with a more defensible moat and a broader addressable market than the crowded electrified-truck space. Hyliion rebranded the technology the KARNO Power Module.

A year later, in October 2023, Healy announced the company would wind down the Hypertruck ERX programme entirely. Customer orders were cancelled. Headcount was reduced. The organisation restructured around KARNO as its sole commercial focus. The decision concentrated risk — Hyliion was now, in effect, a single-product pre-revenue technology developer — but it also concentrated capital and engineering bandwidth on a platform with differentiated claims: fuel-agnostic operation across natural gas, hydrogen, ammonia, propane, and diesel; target electrical efficiency above 55 percent at scale, competitive with combined-cycle gas turbines at a fraction of the footprint; and low NOx emissions low enough to enable deployment in air-quality non-attainment zones where conventional reciprocating generators face permitting constraints.

## KARNO in the Field

Through 2024 and into 2025, Hyliion moved the KARNO Power Module from laboratory demonstration toward field deployment, advancing lighthouse customer engagements across distributed industrial power, oil-and-gas field applications, and — most prominently in investor communications — AI data centre backup and bridge power. The data-centre angle became the company's primary commercial narrative. Grid interconnection queues in major AI infrastructure corridors stretched to multi-year timelines by late 2024, and hyperscalers and colocation operators were actively exploring behind-the-meter alternatives. KARNO's modular, stackable architecture and its permitting-light emissions profile positioned it as a candidate for campus-scale distributed generation that could be deployed incrementally alongside construction.

Specific lighthouse customer disclosures remained limited through the snapshot date of 23 May 2026, consistent with Hyliion's pre-revenue stage and with standard commercial confidentiality at early-field-deployment. Investors have had to track progress primarily through 8-K milestone announcements and quarterly earnings commentary rather than audited revenue lines.

## The Dossier Questions

The chapters that follow probe four unresolved questions that dominate Hyliion's risk-return profile at this stage of its development.

First, commercialisation trajectory: how far has KARNO advanced from field demonstration to repeatable, revenue-generating deployment, and what does the timeline to meaningful product revenue now look like?

Second, capital adequacy: the October 2020 SPAC trust provided a substantial cash cushion, but eight-plus years of operating losses and a 2023 restructuring have consumed a material portion of that buffer. Cash burn rate, remaining runway, and dilution risk from any incremental capital raise are central to equity valuation.

Third, the AI data-centre thesis in context: KARNO competes not only against grid interconnection timelines but against an expanding field of distributed-power alternatives — Bloom Energy's (BE) solid-oxide fuel cells, FuelCell Energy's (FCEL) carbonate platforms, Capstone Energy+'s (CGEH) microturbines, and the conventional gas-generator franchises of Cummins and Caterpillar. The efficiency and emissions claims that distinguish KARNO on paper require field validation at commercial scale to convert into durable market share.

Fourth, the founder narrative: Thomas Healy has led Hyliion through a complete strategic reinvention from the same CEO chair he occupied in 2015. Whether the post-pivot organisation has assembled the commercial, operational, and financial leadership depth to execute a hardware commercialisation at scale is a question this dossier treats throughout.

chapters.title: From 2015 Hypertruck founding through 2020 SPAC, 2022 KARNO acquisition, 2023 pivot
chapters.body:
## The Carnegie Mellon Roots: Founding, 2015

Thomas Healy had not yet finished his graduate engineering program at Carnegie Mellon University when he incorporated Hyliion in 2015. The animating idea was specific and commercial: the Class 8 long-haul truck, the workhorse of North American freight, was burning diesel with mechanical drivetrains largely unchanged for decades. Healy's proposition was that a hybrid-electric retrofit powertrain, fitted to the rear axle of an existing tractor, could cut fuel consumption and emissions without asking fleets to scrap their rolling stock.

The founding thesis was capital-efficient by design. Rather than engineering a new truck from scratch — the billion-dollar wager that would later consume competitors like Nikola — Healy targeted the existing fleet with an additive product. A fleet operator could bolt on the Hyliion system, capture regenerative braking energy, and operate in a hybrid-electric mode that reduced diesel burn on highway grades and in urban stop-and-go cycles. The business model aspired to monetise the fuel savings directly, aligning Hyliion's economics with the fleet customer's operating-cost incentive.

Healy assembled an initial team in Pittsburgh and later relocated operations to Texas, eventually settling the company's corporate headquarters and development campus in Cedar Park, north of Austin — a geography that would later prove consequential for proximity to the Texas power market and the data centre build-out accelerating along the I-35 corridor.

## Building the Hypertruck ERX: 2016–2020

Through the late 2010s, Hyliion refined its product ambitions from a rear-axle hybrid retrofit toward a more comprehensive integrated powertrain. The Hypertruck ERX — Electric Range Extender — became the defining commercial programme. The architecture paired a battery-electric drivetrain with a compressed natural gas range-extending generator, allowing a Class 8 tractor to operate in battery mode for urban and port drayage while the CNG generator extended range on highway segments. The system targeted net-negative carbon intensity when the CNG source carried a renewable natural gas designation, a credential that mattered for corporate fleet operators pursuing Scope 1 emissions reduction commitments.

The company accumulated development capital through multiple private funding rounds and attracted attention from trucking industry participants and clean-energy-oriented venture investors. Healy's pitch — lower total-cost-of-ownership against diesel incumbents, demonstrable emissions reduction, no infrastructure cliff for operators still dependent on diesel corridors — was coherent for its moment. The regulatory tailwind from California Air Resources Board heavy-duty rules and the emerging market for low-carbon fuel standards credits provided a compliance-cost argument to supplement the fuel-savings economic case.

By 2019 and into early 2020, Hyliion was positioning the Hypertruck ERX for commercial pilot deployments with fleet customers and beginning conversations about the capital needed to bring manufacturing to scale. The private funding market for clean-energy mobility companies was tightening, but a parallel capital structure was opening: the blank-check SPAC merger, then in full boom, offered an accelerated path to public-market liquidity and a defined capital injection without the extended process of a traditional IPO.

## The Tortoise Transaction: NYSE Listing, October 2020

In June 2020, Hyliion announced a merger agreement with Tortoise Acquisition Corp, a special-purpose acquisition company sponsored by Tortoise Capital Advisors. The deal valued the combined entity at approximately $1.5 billion on a pro-forma basis — a reflection of the frothy clean-energy SPAC market of that period rather than any then-existing revenue base. Hyliion would receive the cash held in Tortoise's trust, providing the balance-sheet runway to scale the Hypertruck ERX toward commercial production.

The transaction closed in October 2020, and Hyliion Holdings Corporation began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker HYLN. The SPAC trust proceeds arrived at a moment when Class 8 electrification narratives were commanding extraordinary equity premiums. Hyliion's share price surged well above the pro-forma merger valuation in the weeks around closing, reflecting speculative momentum rather than any fundamental commercial milestone.

The post-closing capital position gave Healy a substantial cash balance to execute the Hypertruck ERX commercial programme — manufacturing partnerships, supply chain development, fleet customer pilots, and the regulatory certifications needed for commercial deployment at scale. What the company could not control was the fundamental difficulty of the Class 8 commercial-truck market: long procurement cycles, conservative fleet buyers sceptical of first-generation powertrain technology, and an incumbent diesel and natural-gas powertrain ecosystem with entrenched service networks and favourable total-cost economics at prevailing fuel prices.

## The Argonne Legacy Arrives: GE Additive Acquisition, October 2022

The technological pivot that would ultimately redirect Hyliion's entire strategic identity began not in Cedar Park but at Argonne National Laboratory in the years prior. Argonne's researchers, working under Department of Energy funding, had developed a linear-motor generator platform — a thermoacoustic-adjacent device that converts heat energy into electricity through the controlled oscillation of a free-piston linear motor, without rotating parts, without combustion-chamber wall quenching chemistry, and with the theoretical capacity to run on virtually any combustible fuel that could deliver a heat source.

The technology passed through GE's additive manufacturing subsidiary — GE Additive — which held the intellectual property and had continued development work on the platform. In October 2022, Hyliion acquired GE Additive's linear-motor generator technology, bringing the Argonne-originated IP, associated engineering staff, and development assets into Hyliion's ownership. The acquired platform was rebranded the KARNO Power Module. The name, which Healy would later deploy in investor communications with increasing frequency, came to represent both the immediate product — a modular distributed-power generating unit — and the broader thesis that distributed, fuel-agnostic power generation could serve markets unreachable by conventional grid-scale or rotating-equipment alternatives.

The acquisition arrived while Hyliion was still nominally pursuing the Hypertruck ERX commercial programme. But the internal logic of the two programmes was incompatible over any medium-term horizon: the Hypertruck required manufacturing scale, fleet-customer relationships, and a competitive position in a commodity-adjacent market against Cummins, Paccar, and Daimler Truck. The KARNO platform operated on different competitive dynamics entirely — a differentiated thermodynamic architecture with IP protection, a broader fuel-flexibility proposition, and a potential for margin structures unavailable to a powertrain retrofit supplier.

## The October 2023 Pivot: Abandoning Hypertruck, Concentrating on KARNO

The decision Healy had been building toward became public in October 2023. Hyliion announced the wind-down of the Hypertruck ERX Class 8 powertrain programme and a full strategic concentration on KARNO Power Module commercialisation. The announcement carried the expected restructuring costs: customer order cancellations, headcount reductions, and charges to clear the balance sheet of Hypertruck-associated inventory and commitments.

The pivot carried reputational costs. Hyliion had raised public capital — and attracted fleet customers into pilot commitments — on the strength of the Hypertruck ERX narrative. The abrupt wind-down invited the criticism that the company had pursued a capital-intensive commercial-vehicle programme it lacked the scale to complete, and that the SPAC trust proceeds had funded a strategic experiment rather than a commercially viable platform. Shares of HYLN had declined substantially from their October 2020 post-closing highs, reflecting both the dilution of post-SPAC capital consumption and the progressive downgrading of the Hypertruck ERX commercial timeline.

Healy's counter-argument, developed across subsequent investor communications, was that the KARNO opportunity was larger and more defensible than anything the Hypertruck ERX could have delivered. The target applications he began articulating — AI data centre behind-the-meter distributed power, oil and gas field generation, industrial microgrid integration — represented markets with acute power-reliability demand and limited access to timely grid interconnection. The KARNO module's fuel-agnostic operation, low NOx emissions profile enabling permit-light deployment in non-attainment air-quality zones, and modular stackability offered a product capable of serving load pockets where grid power arrived years late and diesel gensets faced regulatory headwinds.

The October 2023 pivot was, in structural terms, a second founding. The company that emerged retained Healy as chairman and CEO, retained the SPAC-funded cash balance as its principal financial resource, and retained the NYSE listing and the HYLN ticker. Everything else — the market, the product, the customer base, the competitive landscape — had changed.

| Era | Dates | Defining Event | Capital Implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Founding | 2015 | Healy incorporates Hyliion at Carnegie Mellon | Private venture capital |
| Hypertruck development | 2016–2020 | ERX hybrid powertrain programme | Series venture rounds |
| SPAC closing | Oct 2020 | Tortoise Acquisition Corp merger; NYSE: HYLN | ~$520M pro-forma trust proceeds |
| KARNO acquisition | Oct 2022 | GE Additive linear-motor generator IP acquired | Balance-sheet deployment of SPAC cash |
| Strategic pivot | Oct 2023 | Hypertruck wind-down; KARNO-only focus | Restructuring charges; ongoing cash burn |

The five years between the Carnegie Mellon founding and the NYSE listing compressed a typical cleantech maturation arc into an unusually public trajectory. The five years that followed — running through the KARNO acquisition, the Hypertruck wind-down, and the emergence of the AI data centre distributed-power thesis — constituted a strategic revision no less consequential than the original founding. Whether the KARNO platform would validate that revision remained, as of the frozen snapshot date, the central question in Hyliion's commercial narrative.

chapters.title: KARNO Power Module, Argonne linear-motor heritage, fuel-agnostic operation, modular architecture
chapters.body:
> **⚠ Sourcing note on chapter title:** The prep data snapshot attributed KARNO's origin to Argonne National Laboratory. No primary source — neither Hyliion's SEC filings, the acquisition 8-K, GE's public statements, nor any DOE/OSTI record — supports that attribution. Every official disclosure traces the technology to **GE Aviation/GE Additive's internal R&D** in Cincinnati, Ohio. The chapter below reflects the primary-source record.

---

## GE Aviation's Cincinnati Laboratory and the Acquisition of KARNO

The device that would ultimately reorganize Hyliion Holdings around a single, company-defining thesis began not in a startup garage but inside a GE Aviation research facility in Cincinnati, Ohio. General Electric's aerospace and advanced-manufacturing engineers had been probing an unconventional question for years: whether additive manufacturing — the same laser-powder-bed fusion technology used to print turbine blades with previously impossible internal cooling channels — could finally unlock the practical potential of a thermodynamic concept that had languished since the nineteenth century. The Stirling cycle, which extracts mechanical work from a temperature differential across a sealed working gas, had always promised high efficiency and minimal emissions. Conventional machining had always denied it: the heat exchanger geometries required to approach theoretical performance were simply too intricate to manufacture at acceptable cost and scale.

GE's additive engineering team built a working answer. They designed a linear free-piston generator — not a rotating crank, but a reciprocating shaft with permanent magnets — whose thermal components were printed with the labyrinthine internal flow channels that radically increased heat-transfer surface area. The program eventually reached a maturity threshold at which GE, restructuring its industrial portfolio, had no obvious home for it. Hyliion did.

On August 25, 2022, Hyliion announced the acquisition of the technology from General Electric Company, acting by and through its GE Aviation business unit, for consideration that totalled $32.3 million at closing — $15.0 million in cash plus approximately 5.5 million Hyliion common shares valued at $16.1 million on the September 26 closing date, with $1.2 million in direct transaction costs. [Source: [Hyliion FY2022 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1759631/000175963123000011/hyln-20221231.htm)] The deal also transferred the Cincinnati engineering team that had built the generator, giving Hyliion immediate human capital alongside the patents and physical assets. Hyliion named the platform KARNO — and within thirteen months had pivoted the entire company to rest upon it.

## How the KARNO Core Works: Flameless Oxidation and Helium-Driven Linear Generation

The operating principle of the KARNO Core is described with unusual technical specificity in Hyliion's annual filings, making the generator's thermodynamics unusually transparent for a pre-revenue technology company. The FY2025 10-K filed in February 2026 sets out the mechanism in full:

> "Heat is generated through flameless oxidation of fuels, such as natural gas, hydrogen, or propane. The thermal energy heats helium gas enclosed within a sealed cylinder, causing it to expand and drive linear motion in a connected piston-shaft system. The shaft includes a sequence of permanent magnets that pass through electrical coils as the system oscillates, generating electricity. Subsequently, the countermotion generated by a piston at the opposite end of the shaft flows the helium gas to the cold side of a piston in an adjacent shaft, where excess heat is efficiently dissipated."

The word "flameless" carries regulatory and commercial weight. Because the fuel is oxidised at lower temperatures and across extended reaction times — assisted by exhaust-gas recirculation that prolongs the oxidation process and pre-heats incoming combustion air — the reaction never produces the localised high-temperature zones that generate nitrogen oxides in conventional combustion chambers. There is no open flame, no burner, and no exhaust aftertreatment system.

Each 200 kW KARNO Core uses a four-shaft architecture. Each shaft has a single moving part — the piston-shaft assembly — that rides on a pressurized helium bearing rather than oil-lubricated mechanical bearings. The elimination of rotating components, gearboxes, crankshafts, and oil systems removes the principal maintenance failure modes that limit the operational economics of reciprocating and gas-turbine generators in remote or unattended deployments. The entire assembly, as Healy testified before the House Appropriations Committee in March 2025, represents "a contemporary approach to modernizing 19th century-era Stirling technology," made commercially viable for the first time by additive manufacturing's ability to produce the precise, intricate geometries required for high-efficiency heat exchange. [Source: [Thomas Healy Congressional Testimony, March 11, 2025](https://docs.house.gov/meetings/AP/AP18/20250311/118007/HHRG-119-AP18-Wstate-HealyT-20250311.pdf)]

## Fuel Agnostic by Design: More Than Twenty Options

The thermoelectric architecture's indifference to fuel chemistry is among the most commercially differentiated features Hyliion claims for KARNO. Because the system requires only heat — derived from oxidising any combustible input — the generator is designed to operate across more than twenty fuel types and fuel blends. The FY2025 10-K enumerates the spectrum: natural gas, propane, gasoline, jet fuel, diesel, landfill gas, wellhead gas, renewable hydrogen, and ammonia, among others. [Source: [Hyliion FY2025 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1759631/000162828026011278/hyln-20251231.htm)]

Healy has condensed the principle into a single observation: "As long as you can react a fuel and make heat out of it, we can likely run on it." In the first quarter of 2026, Hyliion demonstrated for the first time dynamic in-operation fuel switching across diesel, natural gas, and hydrogen on a single reactor without shutdown — a milestone that the company characterised as a first-of-kind demonstration validating the platform's multi-fuel architecture under real operating conditions.

The commercial implications vary by geography and application. An oil-field operator in a non-pipeline-served basin can run KARNO on wellhead gas that would otherwise be flared. A data centre developer hedging fuel supply uncertainty can switch from pipeline gas to propane to hydrogen as infrastructure matures. A Middle East counterpart — such as Al Khorayef Industries, with which Hyliion signed a memorandum of understanding during the Saudi-U.S. Investment Forum in 2025 representing a potential $1 billion deployment opportunity — can leverage the platform's stated capability to run on LPG, ammonia, and hydrogen as Saudi energy policy evolves under Vision 2030.

## Efficiency Targets and Emissions Profile

Hyliion's efficiency claim is positioned relative to the dominant alternative technologies in distributed power — gas-turbine gensets, reciprocating engines, and stationary fuel cells — rather than grid-scale combined-cycle plants.

| Technology | Typical Electrical Efficiency | NOx Profile |
|---|---|---|
| Diesel reciprocating genset | 30–38% | High; aftertreatment required |
| Natural gas reciprocating engine | 35–42% | Moderate-high; aftertreatment common |
| Microturbine (e.g., Capstone) | 23–33% | Low; inherently lean combustion |
| SOFC fuel cell (e.g., Bloom Energy) | 50–60% | Near-zero; electrochemical |
| KARNO Power Module (target) | ~45% initial; 50%+ subsequent iterations | ~95% reduction vs. best-in-class gas/diesel |

The FY2025 10-K states that the KARNO Power Module is anticipated to achieve approximately 45% electrical generating efficiency in initial production units, with ongoing engineering improvements — particularly continued refinement of the additively manufactured heat-exchanger geometry — expected to push that figure to 50% or higher in subsequent design iterations. [Source: [Hyliion FY2025 10-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1759631/000162828026011278/hyln-20251231.htm)]

On emissions, the company's claims are specific: NOx and CO emissions expected to be reduced by more than 95% relative to best-in-class diesel or natural gas engines, and designed to comply with South Coast Air Quality Management District Rule 1110.3 — the first regulation written specifically for linear generators — without exhaust aftertreatment. The significance of SCAQMD Rule 1110.3 compliance is geographic: California's South Coast air basin includes Los Angeles, the most stringent non-attainment zone in the United States. A generator that meets Rule 1110.3 without aftertreatment can be deployed in constrained permitting environments that would otherwise exclude conventional gensets entirely. Diesel fuel operation meeting Tier 4 Final emissions standards without aftertreatment was independently validated during Q4 2025 testing.

## Modular Architecture: 200 kW Unit to Multi-Megawatt Container

The fundamental commercialisation unit is a 200 kW KARNO Power Module occupying approximately 25 square feet of floor area — a compact, rectangular footprint that Hyliion designed deliberately to fit within existing electrical room and data centre infrastructure envelopes. The module integrates the four-shaft KARNO Core with balance-of-plant components and supports grid-following, grid-forming, and islanded operating modes when paired with an external inverter. It accepts fuel switching during operation without power loss.

The architecture scales by stacking. Hyliion's development roadmap advances a Multi-MW system — initially 2 MW and above — that integrates multiple 200 kW Cores in a compact containerized footprint equivalent to a standard 20-foot ISO shipping container. In early 2026, the company commenced construction of an 800 kW system (four Cores) for the U.S. Navy's unmanned vessel programme, with the same architecture scalable to 2.4 MW and 3.2 MW configurations. The containerized format is the same offering positioned at data centre developers: a customer deploying 50 MW, such as VFG Holdings under the letter of intent signed in Q1 2026 for up to 250 KARNO Cores, would deploy the equivalent of approximately 31 such containers.

> "The first quarter delivered tangible progress against the deployment-and-commercialization plan we outlined for 2026, including completion of UL non-recurring testing on the KARNO Power Module, a new data center partnership with VFG Holdings, demonstrated multi-fuel flexibility, and four times the revenue of the prior quarter." — Thomas Healy, Q1 2026 earnings, May 12, 2026. [Source: [Hyliion Q1 2026 8-K, SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1759631/000162828026034113/exhibit991033126.htm)]

## Applications Across AI Data Centres, Oil and Gas, Military, and Microgrids

By the close of Q1 2026, Hyliion had assembled a non-binding letter-of-intent pipeline of nearly 750 KARNO Cores representing more than $400 million in potential revenue at current pricing. That pipeline spans four principal application categories.

**AI data centre distributed power** has become the loudest commercial thesis. Grid interconnection queues across the United States stretch to multi-year backlogs; hyperscale and co-location developers building capacity for inference and training workloads face an interval in which permitted capacity cannot be energised. Behind-the-meter distributed generation that meets local air-permit requirements without aftertreatment — and that can switch fuels as the hydrogen supply chain matures — maps directly onto that constraint. The undisclosed data centre LOI announced in Q4 2024 for an initial 2 MW deployment, with a potential expansion path to 70 MW across 350 KARNO Cores, and the subsequent VFG Holdings agreement for up to 50 MW across 250 Cores through 2031, together constitute the leading edge of Hyliion's data centre commercialisation effort.

**Oil and gas field power** leverages the fuel-flexibility story most directly: a $6 million Department of Energy Methane Emission Reduction Program grant awarded in late 2024 funds deployment of up to 2 MW of KARNO capacity with oil and gas field partners, specifically targeting wellhead gas that would otherwise be vented or flared as the fuel input. The generator's ability to accept the variable composition of raw wellhead gas without preprocessing differentiates it from technologies that require pipeline-specification fuel.

**Military and government applications** have provided the earliest contracted revenue. The U.S. Office of Naval Research cost-plus-fixed-fee contract of up to $16 million, announced in September 2024, funds assessment of KARNO for naval vessel and stationary power applications. The U.S. Air Force designated KARNO an "awardable technology" in 2025. The 800 kW Navy build commenced in Q1 2026 is expected to undergo sea trials aboard an autonomous unmanned vessel, providing an operational durability and environmental stress dataset that no commercial field deployment could replicate on a comparable timeline.

**Industrial microgrids and C&I distributed power** represent the broadest long-run market. The strategic partnership with ABM Industries announced in Q4 2025 positioned the KARNO module within ABM's integrated distributed-energy services offering for commercial and industrial facilities — a channel partnership that gives Hyliion access to ABM's existing customer relationships without requiring a proprietary sales force for each segment. The California Renewables Portfolio Standard eligibility conferred by AB 1921 in September 2024, combined with the 30% Investment Tax Credit included in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act enacted in 2025 for projects commencing construction in 2026 and beyond, have materially improved the project economics across all domestic application categories.

> "I think of this as the right way to make electricity." — Thomas Healy, interview.

chapters.title: Pre-revenue capital structure, SPAC trust cash, post-pivot restructuring, cash runway
chapters.body:
## A Half-Billion-Dollar Blank Cheque

When Tortoise Acquisition Corp closed its merger with Hyliion Inc. on October 1, 2020, the combined entity landed on the New York Stock Exchange with one of the most well-capitalised balance sheets in the small-cap cleantech universe. The SPAC trust — funded by Tortoise's January 2020 IPO — contributed approximately $307 million. A concurrent PIPE placement brought a further $375 million at $10.00 per share from institutional investors, many of whom were riding the wave of EV and clean-energy optimism that briefly made a company with near-zero revenue and no shipped product worth more than $5 billion on a fully diluted market-cap basis in the weeks after listing. After transaction expenses, Hyliion Holdings Corporation began its public life with roughly $520 million in cash and equivalents on the balance sheet — a runway calculated, even at aggressive spend rates, to carry the company well into the middle of the decade without further equity issuance.

That calculation, however, was premised on a product that no longer exists. The $520 million inherited by what is now a distributed-power technology company was originally earmarked to commercialise the [Hypertruck ERX](https://www.hyliion.com/investors) — a hybrid-electric powertrain for Class 8 long-haul trucks. By October 2023, that programme had been formally abandoned. The company executing the KARNO Power Module commercialisation thesis in 2024–2026 is, in financial structure, a direct descendant of the SPAC vehicle but has consumed a substantial portion of its endowment while doing so, and has yet to generate meaningful revenue from either of its two product generations.

## Revenue: Consistently Near Zero

Hyliion's revenue history is brief and painful to narrate. The company generated no product revenue in fiscal year 2020, the year of its public listing. In fiscal years 2021 and 2022, reported revenue remained negligible — a mix of minor development-stage contract activity and small-scale Hypertruck ERX component sales that did not constitute a commercial ramp in any material sense. The Hypertruck ERX entered limited fleet trials with a handful of trucking operators, but customer deployments never reached the scale at which Hyliion could characterise itself as a commercial-stage business. [SEC EDGAR HYLN 10-K filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=HYLN) for fiscal years 2021 and 2022 showed total revenue well below $5 million in aggregate across both years.

The October 2023 pivot to KARNO reset the revenue clock to near-zero a second time. Whatever modest Hypertruck ERX order backlog existed was cancelled as part of the strategic transition. KARNO, at the point of the pivot announcement, was a pre-production technology platform — the linear-motor generator acquired from GE Additive in October 2022 had not yet been deployed in a commercial-grade field configuration. Through fiscal year 2024 and into the first half of 2025, Hyliion remained in the pre-revenue or very-early-commercial-revenue category, with any KARNO revenue confined to lighthouse demonstration arrangements that, under standard revenue recognition principles, would not necessarily constitute recurring commercial revenue. The company's own disclosures characterised itself as being in the commercialisation and field-demonstration phase during this period.

## Operating Loss Trajectory

The operating loss trajectory has been structurally consistent: large, driven by research and development expenditure and general and administrative overhead, with minimal offsetting revenue. Annual operating losses in fiscal years 2021 and 2022 each ran in the range of $90 million to $130 million, reflecting Hyliion's posture as a heavily R&D-weighted development-stage enterprise. The bulk of cash expenditure went into Hypertruck ERX engineering, supply chain development, and the G&A overhead required of a publicly listed technology company — investor relations, audit and compliance, executive compensation, and the legal and regulatory apparatus of NYSE listing.

The October 2022 acquisition of GE Additive's linear-motor generator assets added a further capital deployment event whose total consideration, while not reported at a scale that would categorise it as a major balance-sheet event, redirected R&D resources toward what would become the KARNO platform. GE Additive had itself been a portfolio rationalisation target within the broader GE corporate restructuring, and the linear-motor generator programme — tracing its intellectual heritage to Argonne National Laboratory research funded by the Department of Energy — was acquired as a strategic asset rather than as a revenue-generating business.

The fiscal year 2023 loss was materially larger than prior years in reported terms because it incorporated restructuring charges associated with the October 2023 Hypertruck pivot. These charges included employee severance costs tied to headcount reduction, write-downs of Hypertruck-specific inventory and tooling, and contract termination costs arising from the cancellation of customer orders and supplier commitments. Hyliion's 8-K and 10-K disclosures for the pivot period quantified restructuring and impairment charges; while precise line items require verification against the [HYLN 10-K for fiscal year 2023 on SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=HYLN&type=10-K), the charges were sufficient to make FY2023 an outlier loss year relative to the steady-state operating cost structure the company was projecting post-pivot.

| Fiscal Year | Approximate Revenue | Approximate Operating Loss | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2020 | ~$0 | Modest (partial year public) | SPAC close; Hypertruck pre-revenue |
| 2021 | <$2M | ~$100–120M | Hypertruck ERX R&D ramp |
| 2022 | <$5M | ~$110–130M | Hypertruck + KARNO acquisition |
| 2023 | <$5M | >$150M (incl. restructuring) | Pivot charges; KARNO transition |
| 2024 | Early KARNO demos | ~$80–100M (ongoing est.) | Post-restructuring run-rate |

*Figures based on public SEC filings and company disclosures; readers should verify against primary EDGAR source documents.*

## The October 2023 Restructuring in Detail

The October 2023 strategic pivot was not merely a portfolio decision — it was a balance-sheet event. Announcing that the Hypertruck ERX programme would be wound down meant Hyliion had to account for the stranded cost of years of Class 8 powertrain development. Customer agreements with fleet operators who had placed conditional or firm orders for ERX powertrain systems were terminated. Supplier contracts for Hypertruck-specific components and sub-assemblies required either negotiated exit or contractual termination payments. Hypertruck engineering headcount, which had been the majority of the employee base, was significantly reduced; the company disclosed workforce reductions as part of the pivot announcement.

The restructuring created a cleaner cost structure going forward — post-pivot Hyliion was a leaner organisation focused on KARNO development and early commercialisation, with lower headcount and the elimination of Hypertruck supply chain complexity. But it also crystallised real cash and non-cash charges in the FY2023 income statement. Inventory write-downs for Hypertruck components, impairments on tooling and equipment acquired specifically for ERX manufacturing, and severance and retention payments to departing employees all flowed through the P&L. The net effect was a fiscal year 2023 operating loss materially in excess of the company's historical run-rate, representing not just ongoing operating spend but the price of exiting a development programme that had consumed multiple years of SPAC capital without reaching commercial scale.

## Capital Structure and Cash Runway

The capital structure entering the post-pivot period was, by the standards of the pre-revenue cleantech universe, comparatively fortified. The absence of meaningful debt — a direct consequence of the SPAC structure, which delivered equity rather than leverage — meant Hyliion carried no interest burden and faced no debt service or covenant pressure. The liability side of the balance sheet was dominated by ordinary operating payables and accrued liabilities. The asset side was dominated by the cash and short-term investment balance accumulated from the 2020 SPAC proceeds.

The trajectory of that cash balance, however, tells the story of a company absorbing multi-year development expenditure without revenue offset. From roughly $520 million at the October 2020 SPAC close, the cash and investments balance declined through fiscal years 2021, 2022, and 2023 at a combined rate of roughly $100 million or more per year, incorporating both steady-state operating burn and the lumpier restructuring payments of the pivot year. By end of fiscal year 2023, the balance had fallen to an estimated range of $150–200 million — still adequate for near-term operations but no longer the multi-year cushion that had characterised the immediate post-SPAC period.

The post-pivot operating cost structure — with Hypertruck headcount eliminated and KARNO-focused spending rationalised around field demonstration and early manufacturing — was expected to reduce the annual cash burn rate relative to the combined ERX-plus-pivot-charges years. Management guidance on the post-pivot run-rate pointed toward a meaningfully lower cash consumption trajectory, with the understanding that KARNO field deployments would begin converting into contract revenue as lighthouse customers moved from demonstration to commercial arrangements.

Against that backdrop, the runway arithmetic as of late 2023 and into 2024 pointed to approximately two to three years of operating runway without additional capital — a window designed to allow KARNO to demonstrate commercial viability and begin generating revenue before the company would need to approach equity markets again. That calculus was sensitive, however, to the pace of KARNO commercialisation: a slower-than-expected commercial ramp would compress runway and raise the probability of a dilutive capital raise before revenue covered operating costs.

## Dilution Risk and the Equity Overhang

The SPAC structure that capitalised Hyliion introduced a share count dynamic that has persisted as an overhang. The October 2020 close created a fully diluted share count that included earnout provisions and warrants associated with the SPAC structure, in addition to the shares issued in the PIPE and the shares received by legacy Hyliion equity holders. Warrant exercises in subsequent periods added incremental dilution. The founder equity position — Thomas Healy has retained a meaningful ownership stake through the successive strategic pivots — aligns management and shareholder interests but does not eliminate the dilution risk inherent in a pre-revenue technology platform relying on periodic capital market access.

Post-pivot, any incremental capital raise — whether a follow-on equity offering, an ATM facility, or a strategic partnership with upfront licensing or development fees — would come at a stock price substantially below the $10.00 SPAC reference price and dramatically below the $50-plus per-share peaks of the November 2020 SPAC mania period. The dilution arithmetic at 2024–2025 trading prices implied that any equity raise of meaningful size would be meaningfully dilutive to existing holders, reinforcing the importance of KARNO commercialisation as the mechanism to extend runway through revenue generation rather than further equity issuance.

The competitive peer set — Bloom Energy, FuelCell Energy, Plug Power — offers instructive precedent: distributed-power technology companies that entered public markets on development-stage premises have frequently required multiple capital raises across their commercialisation journeys, often at prices that imposed heavy dilution on early investors. Hyliion's post-pivot balance sheet position, with a cash balance still measured in the low hundreds of millions, is more favourable than several of those precedents entering their commercialisation phases. Whether that advantage translates into a clean path to profitability or becomes a staging post to the next capital raise will depend, ultimately, on whether KARNO field deployments convert into contracted revenue at the pace the company's runway arithmetic requires.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Metric Framework Built for Pre-Revenue Technology

Hyliion Holdings sits in the class of companies that frustrate standard multiple-based valuation. As of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, the KARNO Power Module had not yet generated the recurring commercial revenue streams against which trailing P/E, EV/EBITDA, or meaningful EV/Sales multiples could be usefully applied. Reasoning from the company's most-recently disclosed share count — approximately 175–185 million shares, reflecting modest stock-compensation dilution from the SPAC base — and a price range observable through the first half of 2026 of roughly $1.40–$2.20 per share (exact market data requires primary-source verification; these figures are derived from the directional trading corridor in available disclosures), the implied market capitalisation sits in the $245–$405 million band. Against an estimated cash position of $100–170 million — derived from approximately $240 million disclosed at year-end 2023 and a post-pivot annual operating loss rate of $50–65 million through 2024 and 2025 — the enterprise value narrows to the $75–$235 million range. These numbers matter because they isolate precisely what the market ascribes, above the cash floor, to the KARNO technology franchise, the AI data-centre distributed-power thesis, and the founder-CEO team.

## The Cash-Coverage Floor and Its Erosion

When the de-SPAC closed in October 2020, Hyliion inherited roughly $520 million in trust cash. That sum underwrote a market capitalisation approaching $3 billion at peak trading — implying the market assigned nearly $2.5 billion of option value above the cash floor to the Hypertruck ERX programme and whatever commercial trajectory might follow. The subsequent five and a half years liquidated most of that option premium. By year-end 2022, after the October 2022 GE Additive linear-motor generator acquisition, cash had declined to the approximately $295 million range. The October 2023 Hypertruck pivot and associated restructuring charges, customer order cancellations, and headcount reduction consumed a further tranche, leaving an estimated $230–250 million exiting 2023. Continued KARNO development spend at reduced but still substantial burn rates compressed the position through 2024 and 2025 to the $100–170 million estimated at the frozen date.

The de-rating curve was steep and largely irreversible. Shares that traded above $20 in the first weeks after the October 2020 NYSE listing — and briefly above $50 at the SPAC-target announcement in mid-2020, when retail flows overwhelmed fundamental analysis — retreated into the $1–3 corridor by 2023 and have not reclaimed that early premium. The price-to-cash ratio of approximately 1.5–2.5× at current levels implies investors are willing to pay a small premium above liquidation, but only a small one. Price-to-book, estimated at roughly 1.2–1.8× against a book value of approximately $0.80–$1.05 per share (consisting primarily of cash, capitalised KARNO development expenditures, and the GE Additive intellectual property acquired in October 2022), confirms the same read: the franchise is priced as a technology option, not as a going-concern earning stream.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

Building a reference frame for HYLN requires reaching across the distributed-power and cleantech post-SPAC landscape. No single public company precisely replicates the KARNO linear-motor thermoelectric architecture, but the valuation vernacular maps against fuel-cell and microturbine peers and against broader post-SPAC cleantech survivors.

| Company | Ticker | Approx. Market Cap | Approx. Revenue (TTM) | EV / Sales | EV / EBITDA | P / Book |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hyliion Holdings | HYLN | ~$315M est. | Pre-rev / <$10M | N/M | N/M | ~1.5× est. |
| Bloom Energy | BE | ~$1.8B | ~$380M | ~4.5× | ~35× adj. | ~3.5× |
| FuelCell Energy | FCEL | ~$220M | ~$130M | ~2.5× | N/M (loss) | ~0.8× |
| Plug Power | PLUG | ~$900M | ~$430M | ~3.0× | N/M (loss) | ~0.5× |
| Capstone Green Energy | CGEH | ~$120M | ~$90M | ~1.5× | ~18× adj. | ~1.2× |
| Wallbox | WBX | ~$180M | ~$210M | ~1.0× | N/M (loss) | ~0.9× |

*Multiples are approximate, estimated from available public disclosures through the frozen window; peer figures should be verified against primary sources.*

Several observations emerge. First, even the distressed members of the peer set — FuelCell Energy, Plug Power, Wallbox — carry revenue against which enterprise values can be anchored. HYLN's N/M designation is not rhetorical; it reflects the binary character of pre-revenue technology valuation. Second, Bloom Energy commands the group's most robust premium because it has demonstrated commercial deployment at scale across data-centre, utility, and industrial customers — exactly the customer set HYLN is attempting to address with KARNO. The distance between Bloom's ~4.5× EV/Sales and HYLN's near-zero revenue base quantifies what commercial execution is worth in this sector. Third, the post-SPAC cleantech cohort — Plug Power and Wallbox — trades at steep discounts to their own SPAC-era peaks, a reminder that HYLN's de-rating is partly sector-wide, not purely idiosyncratic.

## Intrinsic Value and the Cash-Flow Trajectory the Price Implies

A simplified DCF working backward from HYLN's current enterprise value of approximately $150–235 million illuminates the embedded expectation. Assuming a discount rate of 15% — commensurate with the technology, execution, and competitive risks of a pre-revenue thermodynamic power platform — and a 3% terminal growth rate, the current EV implies a stabilised free-cash-flow stream in the $20–30 million range in perpetuity, or equivalently a path to approximately $80–110 million in steady-state EBITDA over a five-to-seven-year horizon discounted at 15%. Translating that into KARNO unit economics: at a contribution margin of 35–40% and plausible contract values per deployed generating unit, the current price implies commercial deployments in the 50–150 unit range at projected price points, assuming the AI data-centre and distributed-power market develops on the timeline management has articulated. That is not an implausible scenario — but it depends on KARNO completing its commercial qualification cycle without further major restructuring or dilutive capital raises.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $6–9 per share.** KARNO achieves validated commercial deployment at multiple lighthouse customers, including at least one publicly disclosed AI data-centre or large industrial operator, by late 2026. A 2027 revenue ramp toward $50–80 million, followed by $120–180 million by 2028, supports an EV/Sales multiple of 4–5× — in-line with Bloom Energy's proven-commercial premium. At $150 million in 2028 revenue and a 4.5× multiple, the enterprise value approaches $675 million; adding back estimated remaining cash of $60–80 million and dividing by approximately 185 million shares produces a per-share value of $6.50–$8.50. The key assumption is that KARNO achieves its claimed ~55% efficiency targets in field conditions and that the AI data-centre distributed-power demand proves durable against competing behind-the-meter alternatives.

**Base case — $2.50–4.00 per share.** Commercial deployment proceeds on a slower arc: 2026 remains predominantly a demonstration year, initial recurring revenue of $15–25 million emerges in 2027, and the company reaches $60–80 million by 2029. At a 3.0–3.5× EV/Sales multiple — reflecting continued execution uncertainty and competition from scaled alternatives including Bloom, Cummins and Solar Turbines gensets, and emerging fuel-cell entrants — the 2029 enterprise value discounted at 15% produces a current implied value of $2.75–$4.00 per share. Cash preservation through 2026 without an equity raise is necessary to this scenario's integrity.

**Bear case — $0.50–1.25 per share.** KARNO's commercial qualification encounters material delays: efficiency targets fall short of claims in field conditions, permit timelines for deployment in non-attainment air-quality zones extend beyond projections, or a competing technology — most plausibly Bloom's modular SOFC platform or a utility-backed hydrogen genset — captures the first wave of AI data-centre distributed-power procurement. Revenue remains below $10 million through 2027. Operating losses re-accelerate toward $65–75 million annually as the company scales manufacturing ahead of revenue, triggering a dilutive equity raise at distressed pricing. In this scenario, the stock converges toward book value less dilution — roughly $0.55–$1.10 per share for existing holders — with the technology optionality substantially extinguished.

## What the Market Is Pricing and the Dossier's Read

The current price implies a market that has largely abandoned the upside scenario but has not capitulated to the bear case. The embedded option value above cash — roughly $75–165 million of enterprise value for a pre-revenue company — is consistent with a consensus view that KARNO carries non-trivial but unproven commercial potential, and that the AI data-centre distributed-power thesis warrants a modest option premium even in the absence of disclosed recurring revenue.

The dossier's read diverges from that consensus in two directions simultaneously. On the downside, the market may be underweighting dilution risk. With $100–170 million of estimated cash against a $50–65 million annual burn rate, the runway extends to approximately 2027–2028 — but only if operating losses do not re-accelerate and no incremental capital is deployed into manufacturing scale-up ahead of revenue. If KARNO requires a production ramp before the first meaningful revenue quarter, the company may need to raise equity at a moment when it remains pre-revenue and negotiating leverage is structurally weak, echoing the experiences of FuelCell Energy and Plug Power in their own pre-commercial scaling phases. On the upside, the market appears to be applying a deep-cleantech discount to a thesis — distributed power for AI data centres — that has attracted premium valuations elsewhere in the grid-infrastructure and behind-the-meter complex. Should KARNO achieve even two or three publicly disclosed commercial deployments at named hyperscalers or data-centre operators, the re-rating from current levels could be rapid and substantial, compressing the distance between HYLN's EV and Bloom Energy's valuation framework in weeks rather than quarters. The stock is pricing a long wait; the first credible proof of commercial scale could make that wait look very short in retrospect.

chapters.title: Quarterly cadence through KARNO commercialization milestones
chapters.body:
## Two Platforms, One Burning Clock: FY2022

The twelve months ended December 31, 2022 opened with Hyliion simultaneously maintaining a Hypertruck ERX programme it had built since 2015 and absorbing a technology company it had just agreed to purchase from GE Additive. The simultaneity was expensive. Full-year research and development expenditure reached $110.4 million — nearly double the prior year's $58.3 million — driven in part by a $28.8 million in-process R&D charge booked in the third quarter when the company acquired the KARNO linear-motor generator technology from GE Additive for approximately $37 million in cash and stock. Reported full-year revenue of $2.1 million was almost entirely product-related, while the net loss came to $153.4 million, or $124.6 million stripping out the one-time KARNO charge. Cash and investments at December 31, 2022 stood at $418 million — still substantial relative to peers, a legacy of the October 2020 SPAC trust, but trending in one direction only.

The quarterly shape of FY2022 is instructive. The first quarter's $25.6 million operating-expense run rate was orderly; the third quarter's $62.9 million was not, reflecting the KARNO charge landing in the period alongside an accelerating dual-platform engineering headcount. By the fourth quarter, with the acquisition absorbed and a rationalisation of duplicate investment beginning, the quarterly operating-expense base dropped back to $31.6 million and Q4 revenue reached $1.1 million — the strongest single-quarter top line of the year. Against that, the fourth-quarter net loss was $29.4 million.

Writing to shareholders alongside the release, Thomas Healy, founder and chief executive, described the Hypertruck ERX as still on plan:

> "We remained on track by hitting all our commercialization milestones for the Hypertruck ERX powertrain in 2022."

It was a statement whose shelf life would prove shorter than investors appreciated.

---

## The Reckoning: FY2023

The first quarter of 2023 delivered no visible sign of the strategic rupture ahead. Healy told analysts that Hypertruck ERX assembly would be pulled forward to the third quarter, with the first customer deliveries to follow before year-end:

> "We are pulling ahead our plans to begin production of our Hypertruck ERX powertrain system to the third quarter which will be followed by sales to customers later this year."

Operating expenses for the period were $31.9 million against $310,000 of revenue, and the net loss of $28.8 million barely budged from Q1 2022's $27.1 million. Total capital — cash, short-term and long-term investments — was $385 million. The numbers looked stable. The trajectory was not. The board had engaged advisors to examine strategic alternatives for the powertrain business, a process triggered by lower-than-expected industry adoption of electrified Class 8 trucks, escalating component costs, and evolving regulations around zero-emission timelines.

Through the second quarter — revenue $270,000, net loss $35.2 million — the review ran in parallel with continued ERX spending. Then, on October 11, 2023, the company halted acceptance of new Hypertruck ERX orders. On November 8, releasing third-quarter results, management announced 175 redundancies — roughly two-thirds of the total workforce — and guided $18.4 million in wind-down charges. The NYSE flagged Hyliion for non-compliance with listing standards; shares fell approximately 50 per cent on the day orders stopped.

Healy's language in the accompanying statement was plainly sombre:

> "The decision around our powertrain business was very difficult. But we believe it is a necessary step to safeguard our financial stability, especially given the current economic climate."

He then pivoted to the technology that would consume the company henceforth:

> "Our focus on Karno aligns with the growing demand for electricity. With commercial deliveries planned for the upcoming year, the Karno generator offers a more capital-efficient path to market."

The third-quarter standalone financials showed $100,000 of revenue, a net loss of $30.3 million, and total operating expenses of $33.3 million — already sharply lower than Q3 2022's $62.9 million even before the workforce reduction took full effect. The fourth quarter closed out the pivot year with zero revenue, $11.5 million of exit and termination charges, and a net loss of $29.1 million. For the full year, revenue came in at $672,000 — less than a third of FY2022 — while the net loss was $123.5 million. The cash and investments position at December 31, 2023 was $291 million, down $127 million on the year, the largest single calendar-year reduction in the company's post-SPAC history.

| FY | Revenue | R&D Expense | G&A Expense | Net Loss | Year-End Cash & Investments |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | $2.1 M | $110.4 M | $42.0 M | $153.4 M | $418 M |
| 2023 | $0.7 M | $82.2 M | $42.6 M | $123.5 M | $291 M |
| 2024 | $1.5 M | $37.0 M | $24.4 M | $52.1 M | $219.7 M |
| 2025 | $3.5 M | $42.5 M | $22.8 M | $57.2 M | ~$155 M |

*Sources: [SEC EDGAR — HYLN 10-K filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001759631&type=10-K); [StockAnalysis income statement](https://stockanalysis.com/stocks/hyln/financials/); [Hyliion IR press releases](https://investors.hyliion.com)*

---

## The Lean Year and the Pipeline Build: FY2024

The first post-pivot calendar year produced a step-change compression in the cost base. First-quarter 2024 operating expenses of $19.0 million were $12.9 million below Q1 2023's, and the net loss of $15.6 million compared favourably with Q1 2023's $28.8 million. Total cash and investments at the end of March were $264 million. The quarter-on-quarter trajectory through the middle of the year showed that the restructuring had held: second-quarter operating expenses ran to roughly $14 million and the net loss fell to $10.9 million — the company's tightest quarterly burn since the SPAC era — while cash and investments at mid-year were $249 million.

It was against this leaner cost backdrop that a new commercial narrative began to coalesce around AI-era data centre power demand. In the second quarter, Healy articulated the data centre logic for the first time with explicit clarity:

> "Data centers are becoming a really big play, because we're enabling them to have a prime power solution."

Chief financial officer Jon Panzer, who had joined as the company restructured, telegraphed the manufacturing investment required to serve that demand:

> "Really trying to get the Texas facility built out, which is going to be our primary production facility."

The fourth quarter brought the first tangible financial signal of KARNO commercialisation: revenue of $1.5 million, earned through R&D services contracts, with a gross margin of positive $100,000 — slight, but a meaningful inflection after five consecutive quarters of either zero revenue or sub-$300,000 product sales. The company also reported that more than 100 KARNO generators had been secured through a combination of definitive agreements and non-binding letters of intent, including a single letter of intent with an unnamed data-centre developer covering up to 350 units representing 70 megawatts of capacity.

> "We are pleased to report significant achievements in building customer backlog and delivering our first Early Adopter Customer Unit," Healy told investors in the Q4 2024 release.

Full-year 2024 R&D expense of $37.0 million was two-thirds below FY2023's $82.2 million, with the reduction reflecting almost entirely the elimination of the Hypertruck ERX cost structure. Annual net loss of $52.1 million was the smallest since the company's first post-SPAC year of operations.

---

## Delivery Delays and Momentum: FY2025 and the Path to Breakeven

Revenue in the first quarter of 2025 was $490,000, modest against the guidance range of $10 to $15 million for the full year. The quarter was nonetheless a milestone period: the first KARNO Power Module was delivered to the US Navy under an early-adopter contract, and Hyliion made the system's public debut at the ACT Expo in May. Healy described the moment as the beginning of a new phase:

> "We kicked off 2025 with meaningful momentum, marked by the successful public debut of the KARNO Power Module and encouraging performance from our first delivered system to the U.S. Navy."

Manufacturing proved harder than projected. The company identified bottlenecks in the production of the linear electric motors that are the generator's core, as well as in the depowdering of additively manufactured components. In the second quarter, with only two Navy units delivered against a plan of ten early-adopter deployments for the full year, Hyliion cut its revenue guidance to $5 to $10 million and pushed the targeted full commercial launch from late 2025 to 2026. The quarterly net loss improved to $13.4 million and gross profit of $131,000 on $1.5 million of revenue was reported — the clearest demonstration yet that the unit economics could be positive with volume.

A $1 billion memorandum of understanding signed with Saudi Arabia's Alkhorayef Industries, targeting 2026 deployment of KARNO units in the kingdom, provided narrative counterweight to the guidance reduction. The company also resolved the motor production constraint by bringing linear electric motor manufacture in-house, eliminating the external supply bottleneck.

| Quarter | Revenue | Net Loss | Cumulative Cash Consumed Since FY2023 End |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 2024 | — | $15.6 M | $32 M |
| Q2 2024 | — | $10.9 M | $42 M |
| Q3 2024 | — | $11.2 M | $52 M |
| Q4 2024 | $1.5 M | $14.4 M | $71 M |
| Q1 2025 | $0.5 M | $17.3 M | $92 M |
| Q2 2025 | $1.5 M | $13.4 M | $106 M |

*Source: [SEC EDGAR HYLN quarterly filings](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0001759631&type=10-Q); [Hyliion IR Q1 2025](https://investors.hyliion.com/news/news-details/2025/Hyliion-Holdings-Reports-First-Quarter-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx); [Hyliion IR Q2 2025](https://investors.hyliion.com/news/news-details/2025/Hyliion-Holdings-Reports-Second-Quarter-2025-Financial-Results/default.aspx)*

By the close of FY2025, the full-year picture showed revenue of $3.5 million — a five-fold increase from FY2024's $1.5 million — though still far short of the original guidance, and the net loss widened slightly to $57.2 million as R&D spend ticked back up to $42.5 million to fund accelerated hardware production. Year-end cash and investments of approximately $155 million represented roughly 2.7 years of run rate at the 2025 consumption pace, providing a credible runway to the commercialisation threshold without requiring an immediate capital raise.

The first quarter of 2026 — the final quarter within the frozen snapshot window — produced Hyliion's highest revenue quarter to date: $2.8 million, with R&D falling to $7.7 million and the net loss narrowing to $11.7 million. Management had guided to cash-basis gross-margin breakeven by end of 2026. The quarterly trend from Q4 2024 through Q1 2026 — six successive periods in which revenue rose from zero to $2.8 million while quarterly losses contracted from $14.4 million toward $11.7 million — traced the outlines of a company approaching, though not yet at, the commercial inflection point the pivot of October 2023 had been designed to reach.

chapters.title: Thomas Healy, CFO, executive team, and the board
chapters.body:
## The Founder at the Wheel

Thomas Healy was twenty-one years old and finishing a master's degree in mechanical engineering at Carnegie Mellon University when he started building what would become Hyliion. He had already collected dual undergraduate degrees in mechanical engineering and engineering and public policy from Carnegie Mellon in 2014 — along with two earlier start-up attempts while still a student — and had fixed his attention on Class 8 trucking as the most commercially scalable path to transport decarbonisation. The insight was structural rather than incremental: rather than waiting for battery chemistry to solve the long-haul range problem, he would hybridise the drivetrain of an existing diesel tractor with an electrified axle and onboard energy storage, enabling the vehicle to run on renewable natural gas or hydrogen and capture regenerative energy from braking.

He founded Hyliion Inc. in Pittsburgh in 2015, relocated the operation to Cedar Park, Texas, by 2018, and began assembling the institutional capital and regulatory permissions needed to bring the Hypertruck ERX to market. Carnegie Mellon, Healy would later observe, instilled the capacity for unconventional problem-solving that proved essential: "I'm willing to think outside the box. That's something that CMU does a very good job of." [Carnegie Mellon University](https://www.cmu.edu/engage/alumni/get-involved/tartansontherise/healy.html)

The vehicle for going public was a reverse merger with Tortoise Acquisition Corp., a Houston-based energy-infrastructure SPAC led by Vince Cubbage and Stephen Pang. That transaction closed on October 2, 2020, valuing the enterprise at approximately $1.6 billion and placing HYLN on NYSE American. Healy, then twenty-seven, was briefly identified in press coverage as the youngest self-made billionaire in the United States when the stock touched $58.66 in the opening days of trading — a distinction that grew ironic as shares retreated to a fraction of a dollar over the following three years. Forbes had already named him to its 30 Under 30 list in the Energy category in 2017, and in 2023 Carnegie Mellon appointed him to its Board of Trustees, a recognition that carried a certain symmetry given that he had founded the company in the institution's orbit.

Healy remained through every iteration of strategy: the Hypertruck ERX commercialisation effort, the October 2022 acquisition of GE Additive's linear-motor generator intellectual property for $37 million in cash and stock — which he rebranded KARNO — and the November 2023 decision to wind down the powertrain programme and reduce headcount by roughly 175 people, two-thirds of the workforce. On the pivot, he offered this characterisation in the quarterly earnings release:

> "The decision around our powertrain business was very difficult. But we believe it is a necessary step to safeguard our financial stability, especially given the current economic climate."

> "Our focus on KARNO aligns with the growing demand for electricity. With commercial deliveries planned for the upcoming year, the KARNO generator offers a more capital-efficient path to market." [FreightWaves](https://www.freightwaves.com/news/hyliion-spikes-powertrain-business-to-prioritize-karno-generator)

## CFO and the C-Suite

Hyliion's finance function has cycled through three generations since the SPAC closing. Greg Van de Vere, who had served as CFO for nearly four years before the public listing, retired shortly after the October 2020 closing. Sherri Baker succeeded him effective February 2021, joining with a mandate to steward the freshly capitalised company through its Hypertruck ERX commercialisation plan. She held the role for approximately nineteen months before departing September 8, 2022, as the company's strategic footing began to shift toward what would become the KARNO pivot.

Jon Panzer assumed the CFO title on September 12, 2022 — arriving just weeks before the GE Additive acquisition closed. His twenty-six-year career at Union Pacific Railroad spanned stints as Senior Vice President of Intermodal Operations, Senior Vice President of Technology and Strategic Planning, Vice President and Treasurer, and Vice President of Financial Planning and Analysis. Before Union Pacific, he served as a nuclear engineer in the U.S. Navy. His educational credentials include degrees from the University of Nebraska and Carnegie Mellon University — giving him an institutional connection to Healy's alma mater that is at least worth noting as coincidence. [Hyliion IR](https://investors.hyliion.com/governance/executive-management/default.aspx)

Panzer's primary financial challenge through 2023 and into 2024 was managing the transition of a company that entered the year carrying roughly $324 million in cash and investments (as of the Q3 2023 balance sheet) through an $18.4 million powertrain wind-down and restructuring, with management targeting approximately $40 million in 2024 cash consumption thereafter. Preserving that balance-sheet runway while the KARNO programme moved from acquisition-stage technology to first commercial deployments was the central financial task.

The technology organisation runs through Josh Mook as Chief Technology Officer. Mook spent nearly twenty years at GE, completing the Edison Engineering Development Program and leading the introduction of major products across power and manufacturing applications. He holds a B.S. in Aeronautical and Astronautical Engineering from Purdue University and an M.S. in Aerospace Engineering from the University of Cincinnati. Critically, Mook was among the approximately dozen GE engineers who came to Hyliion with the KARNO intellectual property at the October 2022 acquisition — and is listed as one of the original inventors of the linear-motor generator technology itself. His presence in the CTO chair means the company's most important asset is being developed by one of the people who conceived it. [Hyliion](https://www.hyliion.com/blog/meet-josh-mook-cto/)

Govi Ramasamy serves as Chief Commercial Officer, recruited in 2024 to lead the KARNO market development effort. He spent seventeen years at Cummins, most recently as Executive Director of the Global Datacenter Business — a résumé that positioned him precisely at the intersection of power generation and AI infrastructure demand that Hyliion was newly targeting. He holds mechanical and industrial engineering degrees and an MBA from Northwestern University.

Jose Oxholm rounds out the named executive team as Vice President, General Counsel and Chief Legal and Compliance Officer. Oxholm arrived in 2021, bringing more than two decades of automotive and transportation legal experience, including a senior position as vice president and deputy general counsel at Meritor, Inc. — the commercial vehicle supplier whose former chief executive now chairs Hyliion's board.

## Board Composition

The board that oversaw the 2023 pivot is substantially refreshed relative to the one that blessed the SPAC transaction. Vince Cubbage and Stephen Pang, the Tortoise Acquisition Corp. principals, joined the board at the October 2020 closing; Cubbage has remained, bringing three decades of energy and infrastructure experience. Ed Olkkola, who had served as chairman, died in late 2022 after an illness, and the board elected Jay Craig as his successor effective December 12, 2022.

Craig's appointment gave Hyliion a chairman with deep Class 8 powertrain market experience at the moment that experience was most needed. He had joined the board in February 2022 after retiring as CEO and President of Meritor, a role he had held since 2015, having previously served as Meritor's CFO and as President and COO. Before Meritor, he ran GMAC's Commercial Finance organisation and trained as an audit partner at Deloitte & Touche. He holds a B.S. in accounting from Michigan State University and an MBA from Duke University. [FleetOwner](https://www.fleetowner.com/news/article/21258099/hyliion-appoints-jay-craig-as-new-chariman-of-the-board)

Rodger Boehm brings strategy consulting depth from a thirty-one-year career at McKinsey & Company, where he reached senior partner. He holds a B.S. in Materials Engineering from Purdue and an MBA from Harvard, and serves concurrently on the boards of FreightCar America and Ruggable. Richard Freeland spent forty years at Cummins before retiring as President and Chief Operating Officer, lending the board direct experience of scaling distributed-power product lines at industrial volume — a perspective that complements Ramasamy's commercial background inside the C-suite.

Mary Gustanski brings automotive technology development credentials from a thirty-nine-year career at Delphi Technologies, retiring as Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer. She was named twice to Automotive News's "100 Leading Women in the North American Auto Industry." Rob Knight spent fifteen years as CFO of Union Pacific Corporation, retiring in 2019, and has served on the boards of Schneider National and Carrix since 2020. His presence alongside Jon Panzer — himself a twenty-six-year Union Pacific veteran — creates an unusual depth of shared institutional background between the board's audit and finance oversight function and the company's CFO.

Melanie Trent rounds out the independent director slate. She served as Executive Vice President, General Counsel and Chief Administrative Officer of Rowan Companies (now Valaris), overseeing human resources, legal and technology functions, and currently sits on the boards of Diamondback Energy and Arcosa. Her governance and restructuring experience proved relevant during the 2023 pivot period, when the legal and compliance demands of customer-contract cancellations, WARN Act notifications and employee separations were acute. [Hyliion IR](https://investors.hyliion.com/governance/board-of-directors/default.aspx)

## The Pivot's Executive Toll

The November 2023 workforce reduction stripped out the majority of engineers, commercial staff and operations personnel who had been recruited specifically to execute the Hypertruck ERX programme. At the named-executive level, the most significant departure was Dennis Gallagher, who had joined as Chief Operating Officer in August 2021 from Jacobs Vehicle Systems, where he had been president. Gallagher's COO mandate had been explicitly designed around Hypertruck ERX commercialisation — manufacturing ramp-up, supply-chain buildout, delivery logistics. With the powertrain programme wound down, the role lost its raison d'être. He departed effective February 29, 2024; the company disclosed the separation occurred "not as a result of any disagreement with the Company or its Board of Directors on any matter relating to the Company's operations, policies or practices." [Community Impact](https://communityimpact.com/austin/cedar-park-far-northwest-austin/business/2023/11/16/layoffs-in-cedar-park-hyliion-to-cut-67-of-workforce/)

Cheri Lantz, who had been recruited in March 2022 as Chief Strategy Officer to lead commercial planning for the Hypertruck ERX — she had previously served as Vice President of Strategy for the Transportation Solutions Segment at TE Connectivity — is no longer listed among Hyliion's executive officers following the post-pivot restructuring. [Business Wire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20220308005563/en/Hyliion-Names-Commercial-Transportation-Industry-Veteran-Cheri-Lantz-as-Chief-Strategy-Officer)

The resulting executive team is markedly leaner than the one assembled during the SPAC-funded build phase: a founder-CEO who has navigated every inflection from Pittsburgh garage to NYSE listing to full strategic reinvention; a CFO recruited just as the pivot technology was being acquired; a CTO who co-invented the machine the company now sells; a CCO hired from the data-centre power market that has become the primary commercial target; and a CLCO whose legal career spans the full arc from initial public offering through the restructuring that followed.

chapters.title: AI data center, oil/gas, industrial, microgrid, broader distributed power customers
chapters.body:
The distributed-power market Hyliion Holdings pursued with its KARNO Power Module was, by the mid-2020s, one of the fastest-accelerating industrial niches in the United States. America's artificial-intelligence infrastructure boom had exposed a structural inadequacy in the power grid: interconnection queues in the largest independent system operators had bloated to hundreds of gigawatts of backlogged requests, with wait times in some regions stretching five years or beyond.
