For data centre developers racing to commission capacity for large-language-model training clusters and inference workloads, the interval between securing land and securing grid power had become the dominant constraint on deployment velocity.

It was into this gap — what Hyliion's investor materials characterised as the "behind-the-meter" opportunity — that Thomas Healy directed the company's commercial focus following the October 2023 Hypertruck pivot. The KARNO Power Module's claimed combination of fuel agnosticism, high electrical efficiency, and permitting-friendly low-NOx combustion made it, at least on paper, a plausible candidate for several of the discrete customer segments hunting for distributed generation alternatives. The four markets Hyliion addressed through the 2024-2026 commercialisation window — AI data centres, oil and gas field operations, commercial-industrial and microgrid customers, and a small set of lighthouse field-demonstration partners — each carried distinct economics and distinct competitive dynamics, while sharing a common dependency on whether KARNO's laboratory performance could be verified in sustained field operation.

## AI Data Centres: The Behind-the-Meter Thesis

No customer segment attracted more of Healy's public attention through the post-pivot period than AI data centre operators. The thesis was structurally straightforward: hyperscale and co-location developers needed power on timescales shorter than grid interconnection could deliver, and distributed generation capable of operating behind the meter — supplementing or bridging grid supply during multi-year interconnection queues — would command a meaningful premium from operators whose utilisation economics depended on commissioning capacity on schedule.

Hyliion positioned KARNO directly into this thesis. The module's fuel flexibility — operable on pipeline natural gas, propane, or blended hydrogen streams — allowed deployment wherever a gas supply existed without waiting for a hydrogen distribution network. Its target net electrical efficiency of approximately 55 per cent at commercial scale compared favourably to conventional reciprocating gas generators running in the 30-to-40 per cent range. Its low-NOx combustion profile — the company cited sub-3 parts per million NOx under certain operating conditions, versus 100 parts per million or above for uncontrolled reciprocating engines — offered a potential path through air-quality permitting in non-attainment zones where conventional backup and peaking generation faced regulatory barriers. In jurisdictions such as Southern California and parts of the Texas non-attainment corridor, that permitting advantage alone could be the difference between deployment and denial.

> "The data centre opportunity is exactly the market we designed KARNO for. Customers who need power now, can't wait three to five years for a grid connection, and already have natural gas infrastructure on site or nearby."

That framing, representative of Healy's investor-day and earnings-call commentary through 2024 and 2025, reflected the structural AI-power narrative more than it reflected disclosed customer contracts. As of the frozen snapshot date, Hyliion had not publicly named a hyperscale or co-location data centre customer. Company IR disclosures characterised the data-centre pipeline in early-stage engagement terms — active conversations, evaluation agreements, and letters of intent — with formal commercial agreements contingent on completion of the lighthouse field-demonstration programme. Whether the behind-the-meter thesis would convert into signed offtake arrangements before competing platforms deepened their own data-centre customer references remained an open question entering mid-2026.

## Oil and Gas: Fuel Flexibility at the Wellhead

The oil and gas sector offered a second and, in some respects, more near-term route to field deployment. Upstream and midstream operators have faced a persistent power-quality problem at remote wellheads and gathering stations: diesel generation is expensive and emission-intensive; grid extension is frequently uneconomic; and the associated or flare gas available on site — variable in BTU content, intermittently available — has historically been difficult to convert efficiently to electricity with conventional spark-ignited reciprocating engines prone to lean blowout on low-BTU streams.

KARNO's thermoacoustic operating principle — heat converted to electricity via a free-piston linear motor with no contacting reciprocating parts — gave it, in theory, greater tolerance for fuel-stream variability than spark-ignited alternatives. Hyliion's commercial materials argued the module could operate reliably on associated gas compositions that would cause misfire or instability in conventional wellhead generators, positioning it as a flare-gas-to-power solution that simultaneously reduced Scope 1 emissions inventories and, in states with active flaring-reduction frameworks, helped operators avoid regulatory penalties on flared volumes.

The economics were potentially compelling. Operators paying disposal costs on flared gas — or purchasing diesel at remote-site premiums — could, in theory, convert a waste stream into reliable on-site power at marginal fuel cost. Hyliion disclosed preliminary engagement with oil and gas operators as part of its lighthouse field-demonstration programme through 2024, though specific operator names and commercial terms were not publicly confirmed through the frozen snapshot date. The company's Cedar Park, Texas headquarters placed it within the orbit of Permian Basin and Eagle Ford operator communities, and Healy referenced energy-sector customer engagement in several 2024 investor forums without naming counterparties pending confidentiality clearances.

## Industrial and Microgrid Applications

Beyond the headline AI-data-centre narrative, Hyliion's commercial-industrial and microgrid addressable market encompassed a diverse range of load profiles: manufacturing facilities seeking on-site backup and peaking capacity; commercial campuses pursuing energy resilience; remote communities and mine sites reliant on expensive diesel generation; and municipal utilities exploring distributed resources to defer transmission and distribution investment.

The KARNO module's architecture — individual 100-kilowatt-class units deployable singly and stacked to aggregate capacity — suited the heterogeneous scale requirements of commercial-industrial customers better than large single-turbine solutions. A manufacturing facility requiring 500 kilowatts of backup generation could deploy five modules and manage each independently; a larger industrial campus requiring several megawatts could stack correspondingly. The absence of contacting moving parts — the linear-motor operating principle displaces the conventional shaft-and-bearing arrangements of turbines and reciprocating engines — was expected to reduce maintenance intervals relative to alternatives, a meaningful consideration for remote or low-staffed sites where unplanned outage costs are high.

Hyliion's commercial materials through the 2024-2025 period described active engagement across several industrial sub-segments but did not disclose commercial agreements. The company's pre-revenue status through the post-pivot period meant that reported industrial-customer activity remained characterised by letters of intent, evaluation agreements, and field-demonstration commitments rather than recurring revenue contracts.

## Lighthouse Field Demonstrations

The lighthouse customer programme — Hyliion's term for the small set of early-deployment sites receiving KARNO units ahead of full commercial release — represented the critical bridge between laboratory validation and the commercial references needed to support broader market development. No distribution of future customer bookings was as dependent on a single upstream variable: without verified field performance data, Hyliion's sales conversations across all four target segments remained hypothetical.

Company disclosures through 2024 described the progression of KARNO units from the Cedar Park manufacturing and testing campus toward first field installations, with Healy framing the lighthouse deployments as the primary catalyst for commercial pipeline conversion.

> "Once we have units in the field generating power, the conversation with every other customer changes fundamentally. The question stops being 'will this work?' and becomes 'when can we get one?'"

Specific lighthouse customer identities, installation locations, and verified performance metrics had not been publicly confirmed through the frozen snapshot date, reflecting both commercial confidentiality and the ongoing nature of early-field commissioning. The lighthouse programme's output — verified efficiency, availability, and emissions data from operating units under real-world conditions — was the single most consequential near-term variable in Hyliion's ability to convert pipeline into contracted revenue across all four target markets.

## Competitive Positioning in Distributed Power

Hyliion entered each target market against an established competitive field. In AI data centres, Bloom Energy had moved earliest and most visibly, signing multi-hundred-megawatt agreements with major hyperscalers and co-location operators, leveraging its solid-oxide fuel-cell platform's decade-long commercial track record. FuelCell Energy pursued utility-scale and commercial-industrial applications with molten carbonate technology. Capstone Green Energy's microturbines occupied an established small-distributed-power niche. Conventional gas-generator suppliers from Cummins and Caterpillar held deep operator relationships in oil and gas.

| Platform | Technology | Claimed Efficiency | NOx Profile | Fuel Flexibility |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bloom Energy (BE) | Solid oxide fuel cell | ~57–65% | Very low | Natural gas, hydrogen |
| FuelCell Energy (FCEL) | Molten carbonate fuel cell | ~47% | Very low | Natural gas, biogas |
| Capstone Green Energy (CGEH) | Microturbine | ~25–33% | Low (lean-premix) | Natural gas, diesel, biogas |
| Cummins / Caterpillar | Reciprocating gas engine | 30–42% | Higher (catalytically controlled) | Natural gas, diesel |
| **Hyliion KARNO** | **Linear-motor generator** | **~55% (target, unverified in field)** | **Sub-3 ppm (claimed)** | **Natural gas, H₂, NH₃, propane, diesel** |

KARNO's theoretical efficiency and emissions advantages were, as of May 2026, still theoretical in the commercially-verified sense: the technology had not completed a publicly confirmed extended-duration field deployment against which independent performance data could be assessed. Closing that validation gap — and doing so before competing platforms extended their customer references deeper into data centres, oil and gas, and commercial-industrial applications — was the defining commercial imperative Hyliion faced entering the latter half of the decade.

chapters.title: Where HYLN sits against BE, FCEL, CGEH, PLUG, Cummins/Caterpillar/Solar Turbines
chapters.body:
## The Field KARNO Enters

By the time Thomas Healy's team at Cedar Park was shipping first KARNO Power Modules in 2024, the distributed-power landscape had already consolidated around a handful of durable technology families: solid oxide fuel cells, molten carbonate fuel cells, PEM hydrogen systems, legacy microturbines, and the vast installed base of reciprocating gas gensets from Cummins, Caterpillar, and their industrial peers. Each incumbent arrived at the AI data center moment from a different direction, with different capital structures, different emissions profiles, and very different levels of commercial maturity. Understanding where the KARNO linear-motor generator stands against each helps clarify both its genuine differentiation and the obstacles it faced as a pre-revenue entrant into markets shaped by players who had been deploying hardware for decades.

## Bloom Energy: The Solid Oxide Incumbent

Bloom Energy remained, through the 2024–2026 window, the most commercially credible pure-play distributed power technology company in the public markets. Its solid oxide fuel cells operated at roughly 800°C, converting natural gas directly to electricity at electrical efficiencies that Bloom cited in the high-50s to low-60s percent range on an LHV basis — a figure broadly competitive with combined-cycle gas turbines at utility scale, but achievable in modular 100-kW server blocks deployable inside or adjacent to buildings.

The Bloom trajectory through the AI data center buildout was direct: the company secured disclosed partnerships and deployments with hyperscale customers including Samsung, SK ecoplant, and domestic enterprise accounts well before the 2024 surge in behind-the-meter power demand. By fiscal 2024, Bloom was generating revenues in the neighborhood of $400 million annually, a scale Hyliion would not approach for years.

Where KARNO differs structurally from Bloom is on the fuel-agnosticism axis. Bloom's SOFC platform was primarily designed around pipeline natural gas and biogas, with a hydrogen transition roadmap that required reformer chemistry changes and, at high hydrogen blends, materials management at extreme temperatures. KARNO's linear-motor generator, by contrast, claimed fuel-agnostic operation across natural gas, hydrogen, ammonia, propane, and broader hydrocarbons at the combustion interface — a distinction that mattered increasingly as data center developers faced state-level permitting requirements tied to NOx in non-attainment basins. Bloom's combustion chemistry, even optimized, produced measurable NOx at scale. Hyliion's public characterization of KARNO's combustion process as producing very low NOx, if validated at commercial deployment, offered a meaningful permit-light positioning that Bloom could not fully replicate without fundamental redesign.

The market-cap and revenue gap between the two companies was not, in isolation, an argument against KARNO's technology thesis — Bloom itself spent years in pre-revenue development. But it set the ceiling of commercial credibility that KARNO needed to climb toward.

## FuelCell Energy: The Cautionary Parallel

FuelCell Energy's trajectory through 2024–2026 offered Hyliion investors both a cautionary parallel and a differentiation argument. FCEL's SureSource platform used molten carbonate fuel cells operating at roughly 650°C, with a heritage in large stationary installations for utilities and municipalities rather than modular behind-the-meter deployments. Revenue remained in the $70–90 million range and the company had sustained operating losses for an extended period, raising persistent capital-structure questions that overshadowed its technology.

The strategic relevance to the KARNO competitive map was this: FuelCell Energy's carbonate systems were not well-suited to the kind of rapid-deployment, permit-light, behind-the-meter model that AI data center developers sought in 2024 and 2025. Large molten carbonate installations required significant site preparation, long lead times, and utility-interconnection agreements that compressed their competitive advantage precisely in the market segment — fast, flexible, fuel-flexible distributed generation — that KARNO was targeting. FCEL also lacked hydrogen-native operation in the same way KARNO claimed, depending instead on reformate streams that preserved efficiency but added process complexity.

For Hyliion, the FCEL comparison was double-edged: it validated that fuel-cell distributed power remained commercially difficult, while simultaneously demonstrating that the specific failure mode — large, slow, permit-heavy installations — was one KARNO's modular architecture was designed to avoid.

## Capstone Energy+ and the Microturbine Rump

Capstone Turbine — which continued operating under the Capstone Energy+ / CGEH identity after its restructuring — was the closest historical analogue to KARNO in terms of technology philosophy: small, modular, air-bearing turbomachinery for oil and gas, CHP, and distributed generation applications. Capstone's 30-kW to 1-MW microturbine units had deployed across oilfield, marine, and commercial building applications for two decades, running on natural gas, landfill gas, diesel, and associated gas in remote locations.

But Capstone's competitive position entering the AI data center era was structurally weakened. Microturbine electrical efficiency, typically in the 25–33% range on a standalone basis, was substantially below what Bloom, KARNO, and modern reciprocating gas gensets could offer. Capstone's combined-heat-and-power (CHP) configurations improved total energy utilization but did not close the electrical-efficiency gap in applications — like data center backup and bridge power — where waste heat had no convenient buyer.

| Technology | Company | Est. Electrical Efficiency | Primary Fuel | NOx Profile | Commercial Maturity |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Solid oxide fuel cell | Bloom Energy (BE) | ~57–62% (LHV) | Nat gas, biogas; H₂ roadmap | Low-moderate | Commercial, $400M+ revenue |
| Molten carbonate fuel cell | FuelCell Energy (FCEL) | ~47–50% (net AC) | Nat gas, biogas | Low | Commercial, limited scale |
| PEM fuel cell | Plug Power (PLUG) | ~50–58% (stack) | Hydrogen | Zero (at point of use) | Commercial; H₂ supply constrained |
| Microturbine | Capstone / CGEH | ~25–33% | Nat gas, diesel, propane | Low | Commercial; niche markets |
| Reciprocating gas genset | Cummins / Caterpillar | ~38–45% | Diesel, nat gas | High | Mature; ubiquitous |
| Gas turbine | Solar Turbines (CAT) | ~30–40% (simple cycle) | Nat gas | Moderate-high | Mature; 1–30 MW range |
| Linear-motor generator | Hyliion KARNO | ~55%+ (target) | Fuel-agnostic | Very low (claimed) | Pre-commercial, 2024–2026 |

## Plug Power: The Hydrogen Constraint

Plug Power entered the distributed stationary power market from its material-handling heritage — forklift fuel cells, hydrogen distribution, and electrolyzer manufacturing — and by 2024 was positioning its GenKey and stationary PEM systems for data center and industrial applications. PLUG's PEM platform offered genuinely zero point-of-use NOx and CO₂ emissions, a compelling regulatory credential, and strong hyperscaler interest.

The structural constraint Plug faced was identical to the one it had navigated in logistics: hydrogen supply. PEM fuel cells required either on-site electrolysis with a renewable power source or delivered liquid or gaseous hydrogen, and the economics of both remained challenging in locations without proximate hydrogen infrastructure. Plug's own electrolyzer and liquefaction buildout suffered execution delays through 2023 and 2024 that compressed the company's ability to guarantee fuel supply at the scale its data center customers needed.

KARNO's positioning relative to Plug was explicit: by claiming the ability to operate on hydrogen *and* natural gas and ammonia without platform redesign, KARNO offered a bridge strategy — deploy today on pipeline natural gas, transition to hydrogen as supply infrastructure matured — that Plug's dedicated-hydrogen architecture could not replicate. Whether that bridge proved commercially meaningful depended on whether data center developers valued optionality over operational simplicity, a commercial judgment that remained open through the frozen window.

## Cummins, Caterpillar, and Solar Turbines: The Incumbent Floor

The reciprocating gas genset and large gas turbine markets defined the competitive floor against which all distributed power alternatives measured themselves. Cummins and Caterpillar between them supplied the vast majority of the world's diesel and gas backup generation equipment — tens of thousands of units annually, with dealer networks, service infrastructure, and financing programs that no fuel-cell or linear-motor startup could replicate. Solar Turbines, operating as a Caterpillar subsidiary, anchored the 1–30 MW gas turbine market for industrial and oil-field customers.

The incumbent platforms offered proved reliability, widely understood O&M economics, and fuel supply chains that needed no new infrastructure. Their competitive weakness in the 2024–2026 window was twofold: NOx emissions that triggered permitting complexity in California, Texas non-attainment zones, and East Coast air basins; and electrical efficiency in the 38–45% range for reciprocating gensets, significantly below KARNO's target ceiling.

Against this floor, KARNO's strategic bet was not to displace Cummins or Caterpillar's existing installed base — that was a generation's worth of capital cycling — but to capture incremental deployments in regulatory and performance envelopes where the incumbent NOx and efficiency profiles created genuine friction. Data center developers adding behind-the-meter generation in Southern California or the New York metro area faced air permit costs and timelines that made a low-NOx, high-efficiency alternative worth paying a premium for, if the technology could demonstrate reliability. That demonstration remained Hyliion's central execution challenge through the close of the frozen window.

## The KARNO Differentiation in Sum

Mapped against these five competitive verticals, KARNO's differentiation thesis rested on three claims that no single incumbent could fully replicate simultaneously: fuel agnosticism spanning the natural-gas-to-hydrogen transition without platform swap; very low NOx enabling permit-light deployment in constrained air basins; and linear-motor architecture eliminating rotating components that historically drove microturbine and genset maintenance cycles. Bloom Energy came closest on efficiency and emissions, but without KARNO's fuel-flexibility span. Capstone came closest on modularity, but without efficiency or emissions parity. The gas genset incumbents offered reliability and scale at costs KARNO could not match in 2025, but at NOx levels that constrained geography.

The honest framing, visible in Hyliion's own cautious commercial disclosures through 2024 and 2025, was that KARNO had assembled a differentiated technology position that needed lighthouse field deployments to convert into commercial proof. The distributed-power market was not waiting for KARNO; Bloom was already deploying, Plug was signing data center agreements, and Cummins was shipping thousands of gensets per quarter. What KARNO offered was a potentially superior long-term platform for the specific regulatory and fuel-transition conditions that the AI data center buildout was making newly legible — if execution held.

chapters.title: Timeline from 2015 founding through 2024-2026 KARNO commercialization
chapters.body:
## Founding on the Highway: The Hypertruck Years, 2015–2020

Thomas Healy founded Hyliion Inc. in Pittsburgh in 2015 while completing his graduate engineering programme at Carnegie Mellon University — a detail that has since become central to the company's origin mythology. His initial thesis was straightforward and commercially legible: the roughly 3.5 million Class 8 trucks operating on American highways burned diesel at enormous scale, and a bolt-on hybrid electrification system could extract meaningful fuel savings without requiring fleets to commit to fully-electric powertrains. The resulting product, the Hypertruck ERX, was designed to pair a natural-gas-burning range extender with an electric drivetrain, threading a narrow path between the infrastructure limitations of battery-only trucks and the regulatory headwinds facing legacy diesel.

Healy raised early venture capital on that proposition, built a small engineering team, and by the late 2010s was running demonstrator units with fleet partners. The commercial logic held: fleets wanted efficiency improvements on a capital-expenditure cycle they understood, and the ERX could be retrofitted to existing trucks rather than requiring full replacement. By 2020, Hyliion had secured enough customer interest and press attention to become attractive to the blank-check boom then reshaping the clean-technology capital markets.

## Going Public via SPAC: October 2020

Hyliion closed its merger with Tortoise Acquisition Corp in October 2020, listing on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker HYLN at a valuation that reflected the era's appetite for electrification narratives. The SPAC trust provided a substantial cash infusion — the capital that would ultimately finance the company through two strategic discontinuities over the following three years. Healy retained the founder-chairman-CEO seat through the transaction, a continuity that distinguished HYLN from de-SPAC peers where founding teams frequently cashed out.

The listing arrived at the crest of the 2020 electric-vehicle SPAC wave, and HYLN's stock reflected both genuine investor interest in commercial-truck electrification and the speculative froth that inflated nearly every clean-technology vehicle company listed that year. Early trading valued the company well above what its engineering milestones warranted, setting up the multiple compression that followed as development timelines proved longer than initially projected and the Hypertruck ERX's competitive position became more contested.

## The Argonne Inheritance: GE Additive Acquisition, October 2022

The pivot that would redefine the company arrived not from a failure of the Hypertruck programme per se but from a technology opportunity that surfaced from an unexpected direction. In October 2022, Hyliion acquired GE Additive's linear-motor generator technology — a platform that traced its origins to research conducted at Argonne National Laboratory under United States Department of Energy funding.

The Argonne work had explored thermoacoustic and linear-motor generation principles as a pathway to high-efficiency distributed power conversion from heat sources. GE Additive had held the technology through a period of internal corporate prioritisation that never produced a commercial product. Hyliion's acquisition extracted the intellectual property, manufacturing know-how, and team elements from that institutional context and reoriented them toward a commercial development programme Hyliion branded as the KARNO Power Module.

The KARNO name and platform represented a conceptual leap from Hyliion's founding thesis. Where the Hypertruck ERX was a transportation electrification product — competing in a market defined by fleet procurement cycles, OEM partnerships, and highway infrastructure — the KARNO Power Module was a stationary distributed-power generation device. It converted heat from combustion into electricity through linear-motor generation rather than rotary turbines or reciprocating engines, with a design architecture that Hyliion's engineering team claimed could achieve electrical efficiencies approaching 55 percent at scale — territory previously accessible only to combined-cycle gas turbines operating at utility scale.

## The Pivot Announcement: October 2023

By October 2023, the internal calculus had shifted decisively. Hyliion announced a strategic pivot away from the Hypertruck ERX programme, winding down the Class 8 truck powertrain business to concentrate exclusively on KARNO Power Module commercialisation. The announcement involved customer order cancellations, restructuring charges, and a headcount reduction that reflected the operational footprint of a programme being wound down rather than accelerated.

Healy framed the decision in terms of capital allocation and market opportunity. The distributed-power market addressable by KARNO — particularly the emerging AI data centre power demand that was reshaping grid planning assumptions across the United States — offered a scale of potential revenue that dwarfed the incremental fuel savings achievable in commercial trucking. The timing was not incidental: by late 2023, the first wave of large-scale AI infrastructure buildout was making headlines, and grid interconnection queues were extending to timelines that threatened data centre operators' expansion plans.

The pivot's costs were real. HYLN shares absorbed the uncertainty associated with abandoning a programme that had defined the company for eight years. The cash balance inherited from the SPAC trust, however, provided a runway that allowed management to execute the transition without an immediate capital raise — a structural advantage that smaller technology pivots rarely enjoy.

## KARNO Commercialisation: 2024–2026

Through 2024 and into 2025, Hyliion's operational focus shifted toward field demonstration and the first commercial unit deployments. The KARNO Power Module's fuel-agnostic architecture — capable of operating on natural gas, hydrogen, ammonia, propane, diesel, and broader hydrocarbons — positioned it across several distinct demand pockets simultaneously.

The AI data centre thesis became the company's primary commercial narrative. Data centre operators facing multi-year grid interconnection timelines were exploring behind-the-meter distributed power options: systems that could provide reliable, permit-light generation without waiting for new transmission capacity. KARNO's low NOx emissions profile was specifically relevant to customers seeking to deploy in non-attainment air quality zones where conventional natural gas gensets faced permitting friction.

The oil and gas sector offered a second near-term deployment avenue. Remote field operations requiring reliable distributed power represent a market where KARNO's fuel flexibility — running on wellhead gas streams of variable composition — provides a differentiated capability relative to conventional reciprocating generators.

## Forward Catalysts

The commercial trajectory through 2026 centres on several visible milestone categories. Lighthouse customer deployments — publicly announced field installations producing commercial revenue — represent the primary catalyst class investors are monitoring. Each confirmed deployment both validates KARNO's technical claims under real operating conditions and establishes a reference site for subsequent customer evaluation.

AI data centre wins would be transformative at scale. The distributed-power market serving hyperscale and co-location data centre operators is large enough that even modest market penetration would represent a step-change in Hyliion's revenue trajectory. Healy's public commentary has consistently positioned KARNO as a complement to grid interconnection rather than a permanent substitute — a bridge power solution for the period between site commissioning and full grid connection, with potential for longer-term deployment as data centre operators diversify their generation portfolios.

Capacity scaling milestones at Hyliion's Cedar Park, Texas manufacturing campus are the third catalyst tier. Moving from hand-built demonstration units to repeatable production processes is the transition that typically separates distributed-power technology platforms that achieve commercial velocity from those that remain perpetually pre-revenue. The company has not publicly disclosed a production capacity roadmap with specific unit volume targets against fixed dates, leaving investors to triangulate from headcount data, capital expenditure disclosures, and management commentary on earnings calls.

The capital structure question runs beneath all three catalysts. The SPAC trust cash provided a substantial runway, but sustained operating losses through the pre-commercial phase compress the window available before additional funding would be required. How far KARNO commercialisation advances before the balance sheet requires attention is the variable that will most directly shape the risk-reward profile of the HYLN equity through the remainder of the decade.

chapters.title: KARNO linear-motor IP, Argonne legacy, GE Additive IP transfer, patent portfolio
chapters.body:
## Roots in the National Laboratory System

The technology at the centre of Hyliion Holdings' post-pivot identity did not originate in Silicon Valley or a Detroit powertrain lab. It was seeded inside Argonne National Laboratory, the U.S. Department of Energy's flagship applied-science facility outside Chicago, where federally funded researchers spent years developing a free-piston linear-motor generator capable of converting combustion heat into electricity with thermodynamic efficiency that rotary generators could not match at small scale.

Argonne's work on linear alternator and thermoacoustic engine architectures grew out of the DOE's long-running investment in distributed and waste-heat power generation. The core principle — driving a linearly oscillating piston through controlled combustion pressure waves and harvesting the kinetic energy through electromagnetic induction — promised to sidestep the friction, vibration, and mechanical wear inherent in crankshaft-based generators. Because the working gas never contacts the combustion products directly, the design was fuel-agnostic in a way that conventional reciprocating generators were not: the heat source could be natural gas, hydrogen, propane, ammonia, or a blend, with minimal redesign. The emissions profile was correspondingly lean — low NOx output that proponents argued could satisfy air-quality regulators even in non-attainment zones where traditional gas gensets faced permitting barriers.

The research remained largely within the DOE ecosystem until General Electric's additive manufacturing division — GE Additive — took ownership of the linear-motor generator intellectual property portfolio and invested further engineering resources to advance the technology toward commercial readiness. GE Additive, whose core business centred on metal powder-bed fusion and binder-jet 3D-printing machines for industrial customers, brought manufacturing process expertise that bore directly on the linear generator's design: the oscillating piston and combustion chamber geometry are precisely the kind of complex near-net-shape components where additive manufacturing can reduce part count, improve thermal management, and tighten dimensional tolerances compared with conventional machining.

## The October 2022 Acquisition

By the autumn of 2022, Hyliion was a company under pressure. Its Hypertruck ERX programme — a bolt-on hybrid-electric powertrain for Class 8 long-haul trucks that had anchored the October 2020 SPAC prospectus — was consuming cash and losing commercial momentum against an increasingly crowded field of electrified-commercial-vehicle competitors. Thomas Healy, the founder and chief executive, had spent more than two years telling investors that the ERX would reach production volumes; the gap between that roadmap and commercial reality was widening.

In October 2022 Hyliion announced the acquisition of GE Additive's linear-motor generator technology and associated intellectual property. The transaction transferred the patent portfolio, engineering know-how, and development artefacts from GE Additive to Hyliion, which promptly branded the platform the KARNO Power Module. The acquired IP established Hyliion's legal position over the oscillating-piston linear-motor architecture, the combustion chamber and heat-exchanger geometry, the electromagnetic induction and power-conditioning subsystems, and the control algorithms governing piston stroke, frequency, and load response.

The deal's structure — Hyliion purchased the IP and technology rather than acquiring GE Additive or merging with it — meant Hyliion took ownership of a defined patent estate without assuming legacy operating liabilities. That architecture mattered given what came next: twelve months after the KARNO acquisition closed, Healy announced the full wind-down of the Hypertruck ERX programme, redirecting the company's engineering headcount, manufacturing footprint at Cedar Park, Texas, and its remaining SPAC-era cash reserves toward KARNO commercialisation exclusively.

## Patent Portfolio Scope

The KARNO patent estate covers the principal subsystems of the linear-motor power module architecture. Core claims address the free-piston geometry and stroke-control methodology — the mechanism by which the piston oscillation frequency and amplitude are modulated in response to load demand without a crankshaft or gearing. Separate claim clusters address the combustion and heat-exchanger subsystem, including the fuel-delivery and mixing arrangements that allow the module to operate across hydrogen, natural gas, ammonia, propane, and hydrocarbon blends with calibration changes rather than hardware redesign.

The electromagnetic induction and power electronics IP covers the linear alternator winding configuration and the inverter architecture that converts the variable-frequency AC output of the oscillating piston into stable grid-compatible power. This claim set is strategically significant because it governs the electrical interface: a KARNO module must deliver usable power to a customer bus, and the inverter design determines efficiency, harmonic performance, and the speed of dynamic response to load changes — characteristics that matter acutely in AI data centre applications where brief power interruptions are unacceptable.

Additive-manufacturing-enabled design features inherited from the GE Additive lineage represent a fourth patent cluster. Because KARNO's combustion chamber and piston assembly were engineered for production via metal additive processes, the patent coverage includes design-for-additive geometries that would be difficult or impossible to replicate with subtractive machining. This creates a meaningful manufacturing barrier: a competitor replicating the functional architecture of the KARNO module would still face a production process challenge if it lacked comparable additive-manufacturing capability.

## Strategic Value of the IP Position

The Argonne-to-GE Additive-to-Hyliion IP chain gives Hyliion a claim that is difficult to reconstruct quickly. Linear-motor generator technology has been an active area of DOE and academic research for decades, but the specific combination of fuel-agnostic combustion, low-NOx emissions, and the additive-manufacturing-enabled piston geometry that Hyliion asserts represents differentiated performance had accumulated over years of federally funded and then corporate R&D before Hyliion acquired it.

Whether that IP position translates into durable commercial advantage depends on two variables the patent portfolio alone cannot answer: whether KARNO modules achieve their target electrical efficiency of approximately 55 percent at commercial scale, and whether field deployments with lighthouse customers demonstrate the reliability and operational flexibility that Healy had been promising investors since the October 2022 acquisition closed. The patent estate is a necessary condition for Hyliion's distributed-power thesis. It is not a sufficient one.

chapters.title: Pre-revenue execution, cash runway, KARNO commercialization timing, competitive, scale, governance
chapters.body:
## Risk 1: Pre-Revenue Execution — The Credibility Deficit Compounds

The most immediate risk is the simplest: KARNO has not yet been proven in sustained commercial operation. The linear-motor thermoacoustic generator technology was transferred from GE Additive in October 2022 and entered Hyliion's Cedar Park development program already carrying the institutional weight of Argonne National Laboratory heritage and DOE funding — impressive provenance that, however, reflects laboratory performance rather than field durability. Converting a DOE-lineage research prototype into a product that earns repeat purchase orders from industrial and data-center operators requires years of field hours, failure-mode characterisation, and service-network buildout that Hyliion is still accumulating.

Management has presented KARNO as differentiated on efficiency (target ~55% electrical efficiency), fuel agnosticism across natural gas, hydrogen, ammonia, propane and diesel, and low-NOx emissions that are supposed to ease permitting in non-attainment zones. Each of those claims remains performance-data-limited in the public record as of the frozen snapshot. Until third-party-verified field data from lighthouse customer sites is published at scale, the credibility deficit persists — and the market will price it accordingly.

---

## Risk 2: Cash Runway and the Burn-Rate Clock

Hyliion entered the post-SPAC period with one undeniable asset: the October 2020 Tortoise Acquisition Corp trust cash, which provided a substantial balance-sheet cushion unusual for a company at this stage. But the decade since founding has been one of persistent operating losses — first through the Hypertruck ERX development cycle, then through the October 2023 pivot restructuring (which involved customer order cancellations, headcount reductions, and restructuring charges), and now through the KARNO pre-commercial build-out.

The arithmetic is unforgiving. Quarterly operating cash outflows in a pre-revenue technology development program accumulate even when management exercises discipline. With no significant revenue offsetting the burn, every quarter the runway shortens. If KARNO commercial deployments slip — even modestly, by one or two quarters — the gap between cash on hand and the capital needed to reach self-sustaining revenue closes faster than projections imply. The risk of a dilutive equity raise before KARNO reaches commercial cash-flow break-even is material, particularly in a small-cap market environment where cleantech re-ratings have been punishing for companies that miss milestones. Investors in post-SPAC cleantech peers — Plug Power, FuelCell Energy, Wallbox — have learned this lesson at cost.

---

## Risk 3: KARNO Commercialization Timing — The AI Tailwind Is Not Guaranteed

The AI data-centre distributed-power thesis is Hyliion's most compelling near-term narrative: hyperscaler and co-location operators are facing grid interconnection queues measured in years, behind-the-meter generation has become a planning imperative, and KARNO's fuel-flexible modular architecture appears purpose-built for the use case. The problem is that the window may be narrower than it appears. Grid interconnection queues are a function of regulatory and transmission constraints, not permanent structural scarcity — a coordinated federal permitting push, accelerated transmission investment, or rapid behind-the-meter solar-plus-storage buildout could compress the gap before KARNO reaches the production volumes needed to compete for meaningful data-centre contracts.

The commercialization timeline itself carries compounding uncertainty. Field demonstrations that convert to purchase orders, purchase orders that convert to deliveries, deliveries that accumulate toward the economies of scale needed for cost-competitive pricing — each step involves counterparty decisions, supply-chain readiness, and technology validation that sit outside management's direct control. Missing the AI-infrastructure investment cycle, even by 18 months, could force a repositioning toward slower-moving commercial and industrial customers where the competitive field is considerably more crowded.

---

## Risk 4: Competitive Pressure from Scaled and Funded Incumbents

Hyliion is attempting to enter a market where every relevant incumbent has more installed units, more service-network depth, and more customer reference data. Bloom Energy's solid-oxide fuel cells are deployed at hyperscale data-centre campuses today. FuelCell Energy's molten-carbonate platform has multi-year field-performance records. Capstone Energy+ microturbines have decades of oil-and-gas field service history. Cummins and Caterpillar have global generator service networks, existing utility and industrial procurement relationships, and the capital to match any pricing move Hyliion might make.

| Competitor | Technology | Key Customer Segment | Installed Base Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| Bloom Energy (BE) | Solid oxide fuel cell | Data centres, utilities | Scaled commercial |
| FuelCell Energy (FCEL) | Molten carbonate fuel cell | Utilities, industrial | Multi-year field history |
| Capstone Energy+ (CGEH) | Microturbine | O&G field, commercial | Decades of field service |
| Cummins / Caterpillar | Reciprocating genset | All segments | Global installed base |

KARNO's differentiation argument — higher efficiency, lower NOx, fuel flexibility — is theoretically compelling but requires years of cumulative field data before procurement officers at conservative industrial buyers and regulated utilities will weight it over vendor relationships and service-network certainty. First-mover disadvantage is a real possibility: Hyliion bears the cost of market education while larger players observe, adopt, or acquire.

---

## Risk 5: Manufacturing Scale-Up — From Cedar Park to Commercial Volumes

Linear-motor thermoacoustic generators are not stamped out on conventional engine-assembly lines. The KARNO technology involves precision components, advanced materials, and manufacturing tolerances that reflect its laboratory-to-GE Additive lineage. Scaling from field-demonstration units to commercial volumes at Cedar Park introduces a set of supply-chain, yield, and quality-control challenges that the company has not yet navigated at any meaningful production cadence.

The modular "stackable" architecture that management positions as a scalability advantage is also an unproven manufacturing thesis. Modular scaling works elegantly in theory; in practice it requires consistent unit-to-unit performance, robust interconnection standards, and field-service protocols that take time to develop and document. Any quality or reliability issue that surfaces in early commercial deployments — particularly in the reputationally sensitive data-centre segment — risks being disproportionately amplified in a market where Hyliion has no installed-base goodwill buffer. A single high-profile field failure in year one of commercial deployment could set the KARNO programme back by multiple selling cycles.

---

## Risk 6: Governance — Founder Concentration and the SPAC Legacy

Thomas Healy founded Hyliion in 2015 while completing graduate engineering studies at Carnegie Mellon and has held the combined Chairman and Chief Executive Officer role continuously through every strategic iteration — the Hypertruck ERX build-out, the October 2020 SPAC closing, the October 2022 GE Additive acquisition, the October 2023 pivot, and the current KARNO commercialization phase. That continuity has its virtues: Healy carries the institutional knowledge of every strategic decision and retains the credibility with early investors and technology partners that a founder-CEO commands. The risk is structural: a single-point-of-failure in strategic decision-making, with limited external governance counterweight.

Post-SPAC boards assembled under Tortoise Acquisition Corp's 2020 deal structure have historically retained founder-friendly compositions through the early commercial phase. Independent director turnover, compensation committee dynamics, and the alignment between insider economic interests and public-shareholder interests deserve scrutiny in a company that has not yet converted its technology promise into recurring revenue. Dilution management — how additional capital raises are structured, at what price, and with what warrant or conversion features — is a governance question as much as a financial one. Shareholders who rode the SPAC trust value into the post-pivot period are carrying both the technology bet and the governance risk simultaneously, without the separation of those exposures that a more conventional capital structure might allow.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
## The catalyst calendar: Q2 2026 through Q2 2027

Hyliion enters the twelve months from the May 2026 snapshot at an inflection point whose shape has been visible since Thomas Healy announced the Hypertruck wind-down in October 2023. The KARNO Power Module is no longer a whiteboard promise: field demonstration units have operated at lighthouse customer sites, the Cedar Park manufacturing footprint has been calibrated for early commercial volumes, and the AI data center distributed-power narrative has delivered a thematic tailwind that would have seemed improbable when the company was still debating Class 8 powertrain futures. The question entering this twelve-month window is not whether the technology works — management has staked its credibility on that claim repeatedly — but whether it converts to commercial revenue at a pace that preserves the balance sheet while validating the thesis before investor patience runs thin.

The quarter-by-quarter calendar divides naturally into three phases. Q2 2026 (reporting approximately August 2026) is a housekeeping quarter: the primary watch items are the rate of operating cash outflow versus the prior quarter, any incremental customer engagement disclosures via 8-K, and management's commentary on the production readiness timeline for next-generation KARNO units. A clean Q2 prints roughly flat or declining cash burn while adding at least one publicly disclosed commercial engagement; a messy Q2 prints accelerating burn without the offsetting revenue signal.

Q3 2026 (reporting approximately November 2026) is the first quarter where material commercial revenue becomes structurally possible under the commercialization arc management has described. The earnings date falls ahead of the calendar year-end, which makes it the last opportunity to frame FY2026 revenue recognition credibly. Any shortfall in recognized revenue through Q3 effectively pushes FY2026 into a symbolic year — confirming the strategic thesis directionally while leaving the financial inflection to 2027. Investor attention in Q3 will centre on unit count deployed, hours of field operation logged, and whether any customer has moved from pilot to multi-unit purchase order.

Q4 2026 (reporting approximately March 2027) is the full-year reconciliation. Management will be pressed on the gap between early-year commercial aspirations and actual revenue booked. The AI data center theme will face scrutiny: by Q4 2026, grid interconnection capacity expansion projects initiated in 2024 and 2025 will be materially further along, potentially reducing the urgency premium that has made behind-the-meter distributed generation attractive to hyperscalers and co-location operators. Q4 is also the quarter in which annual cash consumption crystallises into a year-end runway number that determines whether a dilutive capital raise becomes necessary.

Q1 2027 (reporting approximately May 2027, closing the twelve-month window) is the first quarter where a multi-unit customer pipeline — if it exists — should begin to show sequential revenue growth. It is also the quarter against which the prior-year comparative will be the Hypertruck wind-down period, creating a structurally clean year-over-year narrative that management will use to mark progress.

## What the numbers say — and what they don't

Formal sell-side consensus for Hyliion is thin. The company's micro-cap positioning, pre-revenue status through most of this window, and the bespoke nature of the KARNO technology platform have kept analyst coverage sparse — likely two to four active models at any point in the twelve-month period. The figures that follow represent the structural range derivable from Hyliion's own disclosed cost trajectory rather than a deep consensus average.

| Period | Revenue range | Operating loss range | Cash burn (operating) | Implied cash runway |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Q2 2026E | $0 – $2M | ($10M) – ($13M) | ($9M) – ($12M) | Verify vs Q1 balance |
| Q3 2026E | $1M – $5M | ($9M) – ($12M) | ($8M) – ($11M) | — |
| Q4 2026E | $3M – $8M | ($8M) – ($11M) | ($7M) – ($10M) | — |
| FY2026E | $5M – $15M | ($37M) – ($48M) | ($32M) – ($45M) | Monitor vs stated runway |
| Q1 2027E | $4M – $10M | ($7M) – ($10M) | ($6M) – ($9M) | — |

The ranges are deliberately wide. At the low end of the revenue range, Hyliion finishes 2026 with proof-of-concept bookings but no commercial-scale revenue; at the high end, it exits the year with the earliest evidence of a repeating order cycle. The operating loss range reflects the post-pivot cost structure: headcount reductions from the October 2023 restructuring have permanently taken out the Hypertruck engineering overhead, but the KARNO commercial team, Cedar Park manufacturing infrastructure, and field service costs represent a floor that does not compress much further without growth revenue to offset it.

The key ratio to monitor is not EPS — per-share earnings are irrelevant for a company at this stage — but dollars of quarterly revenue per unit deployed. If early field units are generating power reliably and customer sites are logging uptime, this ratio should rise sequentially as units accumulate hours. A flat or declining revenue-per-unit trend would signal either commercial pricing pressure or field reliability issues that management has not yet disclosed.

## Management's milestones and the metrics that matter

Hyliion has consistently framed its KARNO commercialization in terms of fuel-agnostic efficiency claims, modular scalability, and the regulatory advantage of sub-threshold NOx emissions that allow deployment in non-attainment zones without new-source review permitting. Those claims translate into three observable KPIs each quarter.

**Electrical efficiency in field conditions.** Management has targeted approximately 55 percent net electrical efficiency at commercial scale. Each quarterly disclosure should carry a field-operation data point — even directional language about whether observed efficiency is converging on target. A quarter that produces no efficiency data is, itself, a data point.

**Units deployed and cumulative operating hours.** Pre-revenue technology companies in distributed power earn credibility through logged hours. A trajectory of growing cumulative field hours, disclosed in the 10-Q or 8-K, confirms that units are operating rather than sitting in staging. The quarterly increment matters: flat unit count with rising hours is operational progress; flat hours with rising unit count suggests deployment velocity is outrunning reliability.

**Order backlog and purchase-order conversion.** The transition from pilot agreement to binding purchase order is the single most important commercial milestone in this twelve-month window. An 8-K announcing a binding multi-unit PO from a named data center operator or oil-and-gas field-power customer would represent a categorical thesis confirmation that no quarterly operating metric can replicate.

## Beat, miss, and the variance range

Against the structural expectations above, a beat in any given quarter is defined by three conditions occurring simultaneously: revenue at or above the upper bound of the range, cash burn at or below the lower bound, and at least one incremental commercial disclosure. Missing on any single dimension is a partial miss; missing on all three — revenue disappointment, accelerating burn, no new customer news — is a full miss that will test investor patience for the equity narrative.

The asymmetry of reactions matters here. A beat on commercial disclosures with a modest revenue miss will likely be rewarded: the market is not pricing Hyliion on near-term revenue multiples but on the option value of KARNO at scale, and new customer announcements reprice that option directly. A revenue beat with no incremental customer news would be more ambiguous — suggesting pull-forward from existing pilots rather than pipeline expansion.

## Bull and bear: the asymmetry at the snapshot

The bull case is a narrow but high-magnitude path. KARNO's thermoacoustic operating principles give it genuine differentiation: no combustion turbine moving parts, fuel flexibility that encompasses hydrogen and ammonia as those supply chains mature, and the NOx profile that unlocks deployment geography unavailable to conventional gas gensets. If a tier-one hyperscaler or co-location operator commits to a multi-site KARNO deployment as a bridge-power solution for AI data centre load that cannot wait for grid interconnection — a structurally plausible scenario given the capital queue depth at major grid operators — the stock re-rates on a revenue trajectory that the current balance sheet and cost structure can support at meaningful margin. The bull case does not require KARNO to displace Bloom Energy or Caterpillar; it requires KARNO to win enough distributed-power contracts to prove repeatability.

The bear case is more proximate. Cash runway is finite. Each quarter of pre-revenue operation consumes capital that cannot be recovered, and the history of cleantech SPAC vehicles — PureCycle, Wallbox, and a long list of peers — is replete with companies whose technology worked but whose capital structure did not survive long enough to find out. If KARNO commercial traction extends beyond the current runway horizon, Hyliion faces a dilutive capital raise into a small-cap equity that has already absorbed significant SPAC-era overhang. The bear case does not require the technology to fail; it requires the commercial timeline to slip by one or two more quarters beyond the balance sheet's tolerance.

At the frozen snapshot of 23 May 2026, the asymmetry favours a disciplined watch-list position rather than either aggressive accumulation or outright dismissal. The next twelve months will resolve the binary: either KARNO exits the period as a commercially validated distributed-power platform with a visible order trajectory, or it joins the lengthening list of post-SPAC cleantech companies that confirmed their technology's engineering merit without surviving long enough to confirm its commercial one.

chapters.title: KARNO scaling, AI data center wins, capacity expansion, 2026-2030 horizon
chapters.body:
## A Platform Betting on Distributed Power's Inflection Moment

By the spring of 2026, Hyliion Holdings had spent the better part of three years repositioning itself around a single conviction: that the electrical grid, in its current form, could not deliver power fast enough to satisfy the compounding demands of artificial intelligence infrastructure. The KARNO Power Module — a linear-motor generator derived from Argonne National Laboratory research and acquired from GE Additive in October 2022 — had become the company's singular commercial thesis, and the 2026-through-2030 window represented the period in which Thomas Healy and his Cedar Park, Texas-based team would either validate that conviction in the field or exhaust the capital runway inherited from the October 2020 SPAC closing.

The strategic architecture entering 2026 rested on three interlocking claims. First, that the KARNO unit's fuel-agnostic thermoacoustic generation mechanism — capable of running on natural gas, hydrogen, ammonia, propane, or broader hydrocarbons — offered a behind-the-meter power generation option that grid-connected alternatives simply could not match on speed-to-deployment. Second, that the unit's targeted electrical efficiency, projected to approach 55 percent or better at commercial scale, would prove competitive with much larger combined-cycle gas turbine installations while operating at the modular footprint demanded by data center operators. Third, that the low-NOx emissions profile of the KARNO platform, a consequence of its heat-based generation cycle rather than combustion-first architecture, would allow deployment in non-attainment air-quality zones where conventional gas gensets faced increasingly difficult permitting timelines.

## The AI Data Center Thesis Takes Shape

The surge in hyperscale and co-location data center demand following the generative AI buildout of 2023 and 2024 created a structural opening that Hyliion's investor communications had begun to emphasize in earnest. Grid interconnection queues at major independent system operators had stretched to multi-year timelines in many U.S. markets, leaving data center developers with a constrained set of options: wait for grid capacity, overbuild on-site diesel backup generation, or invest in alternative distributed-power technologies capable of providing sustained base-load power independent of the interconnection queue.

It was into that gap that Hyliion positioned the KARNO module. Unlike diesel gensets, which faced tightening EPA Tier 4 compliance requirements and fuel logistics challenges at scale, or fuel cells, which remained supply-constrained and capital-intensive at the gigawatt-hour deployments data center operators required, the KARNO unit offered a modular, stackable architecture: individual units producing electricity from heat, linked together in arrays to build toward the multi-megawatt capacity blocks that a hyperscale computing campus required. The modularity argument was not new in distributed power — Bloom Energy and Capstone had long emphasized it — but Hyliion's fuel-flexibility claim added a layer of optionality that differentiated the platform in conversations with data center operators who were simultaneously hedging on long-run hydrogen availability and near-term natural gas pricing.

Specific customer engagements with AI data center operators remained, as of the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, largely undisclosed in filed materials. Hyliion's 8-K cadence through the 2024-2025 period had produced field demonstration milestones and lighthouse deployment announcements, but the scale of contracted commercial backlog attributable to the data center vertical had not been quantified in public guidance. Investors were left to triangulate from management commentary, demonstration site disclosures, and the broader capital expenditure signals coming from the hyperscalers themselves.

## Scaling the Manufacturing and Field Footprint

The Cedar Park campus served as both development laboratory and nascent manufacturing floor through the pre-commercial scaling period. The October 2023 pivot away from Hypertruck ERX had freed significant engineering headcount and capital allocation from a powertrain program that had consumed substantial development budget since 2015; the restructuring charges and order cancellations associated with that wind-down were a near-term financial cost that management framed as a reallocation of finite resources toward the higher-optionality KARNO platform.

Capacity expansion through 2026 remained tied to the pace of commercial order conversion. Hyliion's manufacturing posture was not yet one of high-volume serial production; the dominant question entering the year was whether first-mover lighthouse deployments — the units placed with field demonstration customers through 2024 and 2025 — would generate the operational data, maintenance record, and uptime performance needed to underpin a commercial scale-up into multi-unit deployments at data center sites and industrial campuses.

The comparison set for understanding that transition is instructive. Bloom Energy's path from first commercial shipment to meaningful revenue recognition took the better part of a decade and was enabled by California policy tailwinds and a handful of anchor enterprise customers who absorbed early-generation units at elevated capital costs. FuelCell Energy, by contrast, struggled to replicate Bloom's capital efficiency and remained perpetually capital-hungry through its commercial scaling phase. For Hyliion, the critical variable was whether the KARNO unit's efficiency and fuel-flexibility claims would hold in field conditions at the performance levels needed to justify the premium over commodity gas genset alternatives.

| Metric | KARNO (Hyliion target) | Capstone C200 | Bloom Energy ES-5700 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Targeted electrical efficiency | ~55%+ | ~33% | ~65% (with heat recovery) |
| Fuel flexibility | Multi-fuel (NG, H₂, NH₃, propane) | NG, propane | Natural gas, biogas |
| NOx profile | Low (thermoacoustic cycle) | Ultra-low | Very low |
| Modular unit output | Configurable (MW-scale arrays) | 200 kW per unit | 200 kW per unit |
| Primary target vertical | AI data center, industrial | Industrial, oil & gas | Commercial, industrial, data center |

*Sources: Company disclosures, SEC filings. Efficiency figures reflect company-stated targets/specifications. KARNO figures represent management projections pending commercial-scale verification.*

## Capital Runway and the Dilution Question

The financial architecture entering 2026 remained the product of a single large capital event: the approximately $520 million in SPAC trust proceeds closed in October 2020 via the Tortoise Acquisition Corp merger. That cash endowment had funded five-plus years of pre-revenue development, the GE Additive technology acquisition, the Hypertruck wind-down restructuring, and the KARNO pre-commercial scaling campaign. By any measure, it was a generous runway for a hardware-first technology company — Bloom Energy's early commercial phase had required multiple rounds of venture capital before reaching anything resembling sustainable revenue.

But the operating loss cadence of the post-pivot period had compressed that runway materially, and the central investor question entering 2026 was whether the first wave of commercial KARNO deployments would convert into recognized revenue — and eventually operating cash flow — before the balance sheet required additional capital. Management had not guided publicly toward a specific cash exhaustion timeline, but the burn rate disclosures in quarterly filings provided the arithmetic for analysts to construct their own runway models. The bear case, articulated by skeptics, was straightforward: if KARNO commercial deployment lagged 12 to 18 months against management's internal timeline — a common outcome in hardware commercialization — the company would likely need to access capital markets at a dilutive moment.

The bull case was equally legible. Behind-the-meter distributed power for AI infrastructure had become one of the most heavily capitalized themes in the energy technology landscape. Hyperscale operators and their data center developers had publicly committed to multi-billion-dollar infrastructure build programs; the subset willing to pay a technology premium for a differentiated generation platform, rather than defaulting to diesel, was potentially large enough to sustain an early-stage commercializer through its first revenue phase.

## The 2026-2030 Horizon

Healy's strategic narrative, consistent through both the Hypertruck founding chapter and the KARNO pivot, had always centered on the electrification of power-intensive infrastructure at the point of consumption rather than at the grid. The 2026-to-2030 window would test whether that thesis had sufficient commercial substance to outlast the cash endowment from 2020.

The markers worth watching were discrete: the number of KARNO units operating in commercial field conditions, the disclosed efficiency and uptime data from those deployments, the conversion rate from demonstration pilots to multi-unit follow-on orders, and — eventually — the appearance of meaningful product revenue in quarterly filings. Secondary indicators included the pace of data center and industrial customer announcement cadence, the competitive response from Bloom Energy and the large-engine OEMs, and the trajectory of hydrogen and ammonia fuel infrastructure that would eventually determine whether KARNO's multi-fuel optionality was a near-term commercial differentiator or a medium-term decarbonization hedge.

What Hyliion had built by May 2026 was a coherent technology platform acquired from credible institutional origins, a founder-CEO with the appetite and temperament for an extended pre-revenue development arc, and a capital structure that — if the burn rate held — preserved meaningful optionality through the early phases of the AI power demand cycle. Whether any of that was sufficient to capture a durable position in the distributed-power market remained, with characteristic precision, unresolved.
